en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Khandha Vagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Saṃyutta Nikāya: Khandha Saṃyutta 1.
Nakulapitu Vagga 1. Commentary on the Nakulapitu Sutta (The Discourse to Nakula’s Father)

1. The Bhaggas were royal princes from the countryside. Because their entire inhabited territory was conventionally referred to by the singular name "Bhaggā," it is said, "in the country of that name";

the meaning is: "in that [territory] which had acquired its name through the plural [designation]. "In that forest grove" refers to the forest grove that had previously been granted as a sanctuary for deer.
In the forest grove. Because that householder was known in that city as "Nakulapitā" (Father of Nakula) on account of his son, it is said, "Nakulapitā";
the meaning is "the father of a boy named Nakula. His wife was also known as "Nakulamātā" (Mother of Nakula).
"Worn out by old age" means worn out by the process of aging, not worn out by illness and so forth. "Advanced in years" [is said] because of being worn out.

He is "grown old" by having reached the increase of age, not by the increase of virtue and so forth. He is "advanced in years" because of the greatness of his birth and the long duration [of his life].
"One who has gone through the three stages" means one who has traversed the three periods: the first, the middle, and the last.
Therein, because he has transcended the first and the second and has approached the last, he has "reached the final stage. "With a sick body" is due to being overwhelmed by painful sensations.
It is the "non-nourishing body. Furthermore, because illness has suffering as its destination, it is called the "sick body.

For this reason, in the *Saccavibhaṅga* (Analysis of the Truths), within the exposition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), disease is not mentioned separately, as it is already included by the very mention of suffering.

"In the sense of constant oozing" means by way of its state of constantly oozing impurities. As for the phrase "by way of its state of being afflicted," he says: "It is indeed called 'afflicted' (*ātura*)."
"Visesena" means by way of excess. "Ātura" means one who is afflicted; it refers to one whose body is heated up upon entering battle. "Jarāturatā" is the state of being afflicted by old age.
"Manobhāvanīyā" means those who develop the mind through the increase of the wholesome side (kusala-pakkha).
Alternatively, they are called "manobhāvanīyā" because they are to be cultivated or honored by the mind. Regarding "anusāsatu," he said that the meaning here is "let him instruct repeatedly."
“*Punappunaṃ sāsatū*”: this refers to beneficial speech that has been set forth repeatedly and successively.
When a matter has not yet been fully resolved, the statement regarding what constitutes a virtue or a fault for one who acts in such a way is intended.
“By way of the lineage” (*tantivasena*) means that this instruction is so called because it relies upon the lineage (*tanti*). “Tradition” (*paveṇī*) is a synonym for the lineage itself.

“Like an egg, so is the being”: this is an additional simile because the body is more fragile and weaker than the shell of an egg. Thus he said, “An egg,” and so forth. Only a fool, possessing such a state of existence, would claim health for even a moment.
“Clear” means they have transcended their ordinary appearance and are exceptionally clear. Thus he said, “Very clear.
Because of those perfections of form originating from a clear mind, there is the purity of his facial complexion; thus he said, “Purified.”
“Free from defilement. For this very reason he said, “by way of being free from secondary defilements,” and so forth.

By this alone, it should be understood that the cause for the clarity of his faculties has also been described. “This is the color of his face; indeed, it is the wisdom that grasps the guiding principles”—this was said with reference to the fact that it occurs even without the process of adverting the mind.

The passage beginning with "What neither for a son... and so forth is stated specifically with reference to the words spoken [by the sons]: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One exhort us so that we might meet one another even in the world beyond.

Since it was obtained directly from the Teacher’s presence through his sweet teaching of the Dhamma alone, and because it was grasped by their own affection and reverence, it should be understood as "the consecration of the Deathless" (*amatābhiseka*).
These are two words. Because of being far from defilements (*kilesa*), due to having been eradicated by the Path (*magga*).

"In misfortune" (*anaye*) means in non-prosperity; the meaning is "in what is harmful" (*anatthe*). Or, it means in misfortune or in what is not a proper means (*anupāya*). "Because of not proceeding" (*na iriyanato*) means because of not turning toward [the goal]. "In prosperity" (*aye*) means in prosperity, in what is beneficial (*attha*), and in a proper means.

"Because of being worthy of service" (*araṇīyato*) means because of being worthy of attendance. The derivation of the word should be understood according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*) in the preceding alternative explanations of its meaning.

Furthermore, [the term] is also used according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). Although the word *ariya* applies even to worldlings (*puthujjana*) in contexts such as, “Those noble ones whose bodily actions are purified,” because it refers to those with pure intentions and applications, here the author says “and the Buddhas,” etc., showing that what is intended is the state of being noble (*ariyabhāva*) by virtue of having attained the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) and by virtue of being entirely supramundane.
In that context, “paccekabuddhas” refers to the disciples of the Tathāgata.
And the phrase "and true persons" is stated in order to show, without confusion, the meaning of the terms "noble ones" and "true persons" as they are used here.
However, because the states of being noble and being a true person are, in the ultimate sense, identical in nature, it is said, "or rather, all [are one]," and so forth.
Up to this point, the disciple of the Buddha has been described; for he must absolutely have a virtuous friend, as will be explained further on.
Because the first path does not arise apart from the lineage (ghosa). Specifically, it is the Blessed One alone who is intended by the term "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta).
For this has been said: "Ānanda, it is by coming to me as a good friend that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth," and so forth.
And he alone is called one of "firm devotion" through the attainment of verified confidence (aveccapasāda). This too has been said:
“Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their lives.

Regarding the terms *kataññū* and *katavedī*, which refer to *paccekabuddhas* and *buddhas*: here, one who knows what has been done is *kataññū*. One who makes known—that is, makes clear—what has been done is *katavedī*.
For *paccekabuddhas* know the assistance rendered to them even over many hundreds of thousands of eons.
And they make their gratitude manifest by accepting gifts, providing reminders, and so forth.
Likewise, they diligently perform for one who is suffering from the misery of *saṃsāra* whatever service they themselves are capable of performing.

But the Perfectly Enlightened One knows the assistance rendered even throughout thousands of incalculable eons, as well as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the paths and fruits; He makes that gratitude manifest, like a lion.
And thus, by giving the teaching of the Dhamma with thorough attention in every respect, they perform the work of a Buddha.

It should be understood that failing to practice that very way of conduct through which the Noble Ones are seen, and lacking reverence for it, constitutes the habit of not seeing the Noble Ones and not acting skillfully toward their vision. Regarding the phrase "not seeing with the eye":
“Eye” does not mean merely the physical eye; rather, it refers to the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), as indicated by the phrase “or with the divine eye.
“Noble state” (*ariyabhāva*) should be understood as those states of the path and its fruition through association with which one is called “noble” (*ariya*).

In this context, “therein” (*tatra*) refers to the very fact that knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassana*) constitutes seeing. “Basis” (*vatthu*) means the reason for making known the intended meaning. Thus...
"Even when spoken" means even when it has been spoken by applying it to oneself through such an indirect designation (*aññāpadesa*).

"Dhamma" refers to the supramundane dhamma, or the dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. The "dhammas that produce the noble state" (*ariyakara-dhammā*) are the contemplations of impermanence and so forth; or, they are the impermanence and other characteristics being contemplated through insight;
or, they are the Four Noble Truths.
“Untrained” (*avinīta*) means not trained; that is, not disciplined by way of the training in higher virtue and so forth.
To show those restraints and disciplines (*vinaya*) in the absence of which one is called “untrained,” he says: “Discipline is of two kinds,” and so forth.
Therein, “restraint of virtue” (*sīlasaṃvara*) should be understood as the restraint of the Pātimokkha; and in its actual sense, it is the non-transgression of body and speech.
Restraint by mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*) is the guarding of the sense faculties, and that is simply mindfulness as it occurs in such a manner.

Restraint by knowledge (*ñāṇasaṃvara*) should be understood as the restraint, the closing off, and the eradication-knowledge of craving, views, misconduct, ignorance, and the remaining defilements—which are designated as "streams"—as stated in the passage: "I declare the restraint of streams;
they are closed off by wisdom. Restraint by patience (*khantisamvara*) is endurance, and that is...

Some say that "wisdom" refers to the aggregates as they thus proceed, or to non-hatred. Restraint through energy is simply the energy itself proceeding by way of the removal of sensual thoughts and so forth.
Abandonment by means of a particular factor is "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).
Abandonment by way of suppression is "abandonment by suppression" (*vikkhambhanappahāna*). The same method applies to the remaining three terms as well.

“By this restraint of the Pātimokkha,” and so forth, is an exposition of the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara) and the others. Therein, in the word *samupeto*, the particle *iti* has the sense of “beginning with.
By that, it indicates the analysis of restraint (*saṃvara-vibhaṅga*) as it appears in the Vibhaṅga, beginning with the words “approached” (*upagato*).
“Of bodily misconduct, etc. refers to bodily and verbal misconduct reckoned as immorality, to negligence reckoned as forgetfulness (*muṭṭhasacca*), and to covetousness, etc.
Or [it refers to] impatience, ignorance, and indolence. "By restraint" means by closing off;

"by training" means by training the body, speech, and mind away from improper activity, or by removing bodily misconduct and so forth, or by cutting off the crooked course of the body and so on and leading them toward rectitude.
This refers to bodily misconduct and the like which are liable to arise when the necessary conditions coincide.
In that very way, non-arising itself should be understood as restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*) and as leading away (*vinayana*).
This is to be connected with the word "abandonment" (*pahāna*). Why was it said, "in the insight-knowledges such as the discernment of name-and-form"?

Is it not the case that the discernment of name-and-form, the comprehension of conditions, and the overcoming of doubt are not insight-knowledges in the sense of being modes of contemplation (*sammasanākāra*)?
"Because it does not proceed"? This is true; however, it is stated thus because it serves as the foundation for insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).
The discernment of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*) is the knowledge that proceeds thus: "This is merely mind-and-body; herein there is no self or anything belonging to a self.
When the body—consisting of the five aggregates—is present, or when there is a view regarding that body itself, that is the embodiment-view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).

And that is the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) which occurs in the form: “One regards form as self. The discernment of the conditions for that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), such as karma and ignorance, is the discernment of conditions (*paccayapariggaha*).
The view of no cause (*ahetudiṭṭhi*) occurs in the manner: “There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings,” and so forth.
[The view that] “the world proceeds and ceases through God, Puruṣa, Pajāpati, primordial matter, atoms, time, and so on” [is the view of a first cause].
The view that occurs in such and such a manner is the "view of uneven causes. "Of that very [person]" means of one who has already discerned the conditions.

"By the overcoming of doubt" means by the knowledge that removes uncertainty regarding the three periods of time—namely, that just as the arising of name-and-form from conditions such as kamma occurs now, so it occurred in the past and will occur in the future.
"Of the state of being a sceptic" refers to the tendency to proceed according to the mode: "Did I exist in the past? and so forth.

"By the occurrence of doubt": by means of insight-knowledge proceeding through the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*), which consists of casting the five aggregates into the eleven bases according to the formula, "Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present," and so forth.

"Of the grasping 'I' and 'mine'" means of the apprehension of "self" and "belonging to self. "By the definition of the path and the non-path" means by means of the purification of knowledge regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇavisuddhi*).
"Perception of a path where there is no path" means the perception that arises regarding non-paths such as the illumination (obhāsa) and so forth, thinking "this is the path.

Because one who sees the arising of formations correctly grasps that "thus these formations arise from their corresponding causes, but they are not annihilated," it is therefore said: "by seeing the arising [one abandons] the annihilation view. Furthermore, because...

For one who sees the passing away of formations—thinking, "Even if these formations proceed without interruption, yet as they arise, they cease without reconnection"—how could there be a view of eternalism?
Therefore it is said: "By seeing their passing away, [one abandons] the eternalist view. "By seeing the danger" means by the knowledge that apprehends them as fearful.
"In all that is fearful" refers to [the path], because it is the source of the cessation of all fear, which is to say, the subsiding of all suffering.

And because it is the opposite of supreme reassurance, regarding the five aggregates which are fraught with danger, there is the "perception of fearlessness"—that is, the perception arisen [thinking], "This is fearless and secure.
The "perception of gratification" is the perception that occurs by way of finding gratification in the five aggregates of clinging;
it is also called "clinging and adherence. The "perception of delight" is the perception that occurs by way of taking delight in those very same aggregates.
That which is also called "delight" (*nandī*). Grasping (*ādāna*) is the desire not to let go. Non-equanimity (*anupekkhā*) is the failure to feel revulsion toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);

the meaning is "possessing attachment. Regarding the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhiti*), that is, dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), it is the state of inversion, namely the grasping of eternalism or annihilationism, or else the delusion (*moha*) that obscures the mode of conditions.
Regarding Nibbāna, the state of inversion is the inclination toward conditioned phenomena; it is the delusion that obscures Nibbāna.
Or: "Grasping at the sign of formations" refers to that defilement which, due to its non-abandonment, prevents insight from relinquishing the sign of formations;
it is also called "clinging to conjunction. Alternatively, abandonment is simply the transcending of this grasping at the sign of formations.
“Occurrence itself is the state of occurrence”; the meaning is “obsession.

By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “of the phenomena such as the hindrances,” the defilements belonging to the side of the hindrances, as well as applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth, are included.

The connection is: “that abandonment which occurs through the absolute non-occurrence [of those phenomena] due to the cultivation of the four noble paths. But by what means is there abandonment? “By the noble paths themselves.”

This meaning is understood because it is stated that there is no further occurrence due to their having developed [the path]. Regarding the phrase "of that which belongs to the side of origination" (*samudayapakkhikassa*):

here, since all four paths constitute the realization of the Four Truths, they are to be abandoned together with the various forms of greed designated as "origination" (*samudaya*), both because they are to be abandoned by those [paths] and because they share the nature of origination. And in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, all defilements...
Because the state of origination has been described, "belonging to the side of origination" refers to views and so forth. "Allayedness" is the state of being stilled.
"Being escaped from the conditioned" is the absence of the intrinsic nature of formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"Abandoned all that is conditioned" means devoid of everything conditioned; the meaning is "without formations" (*visaṅkhāra*). And because it is both abandonment and discipline, it is "abandonment-discipline" (*pahānavinaya*) in the first sense. In the second sense...
"Abandonment" (*pahāna*) means that which is abandoned; it should be construed with "its discipline" (*tassa vinayo*).
"Because of the broken restraint" (*bhinna-saṃvarattā*) means because of the lost restraint; the meaning is "due to the absence of restraint.
By this, even one who has not formally undertaken restraint is included. For restraint is to be accomplished through formal undertaking; in its absence, it does not exist. "Ariya" [means...].
“Ariya” is a term used in the singular (paccattavacana). “Esesa” means this very one; the meaning is that he is not other than that in substance.
“Tajjāta” means having that same nature in substance; the meaning is that the true person has the nature of the noble one, and the noble one has the nature of the true person.
“So aham” is what the proponent of a wrong view says of himself, imagining a self by way of the notion of “I. It is bound up with the conceit of “I.”
For "self" is the tenet of those who maintain the doctrine of self (*attavādin*). "Non-dual" means devoid of duality.

Just as one who perceives the non-distinction between the flame and the color, grasping the color itself as "flame," sees their identity by thinking "the flame is indeed the color," so too should it be understood that one who perceives their identity grasps the self as imagined—whether as "form" or as the form as it is seen—as "self."

And here, although there is no actual occurrence of the thought "form is self," the grasping at a self in form as it occurs is called "seeing non-duality," just like the grasping at color in a painting.
Furthermore, the similes are stated solely to demonstrate the grasping [of form, etc.

as not being other than [the self], and not for the purpose of showing that a self actually exists in the way that color and so forth exist. For [it is not the case that] in the self, by way of ownership...

One regards form as having the nature of something possessed (*sakiñcana*). Or, one regards form as the self (*attānaṃ rūpassa*) by way of the self being the substratum for form through its own intrinsic nature.
Or, one regards the self as being in form (*rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ*) by way of the self being the substratum for form; this is seen through the vision of wrong view (*diṭṭhipassanā*).

One who dwells obsessed (*pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī*) means one who, through views and craving that have reached the state of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), [regards] "form is the self" or "one possessed of form."
Because one persists by wrongly grasping the pentad of aggregates as "self" and so forth. Therefore he said, "in the mode of obsession," and so on.

"The same method" means that just as the method of commentary was stated regarding the aggregate of form in the passage beginning, "Here someone regards form as self," this very same method is to be understood for the aggregate of feeling and the others as well.
"Pure form alone" means form exclusively, unmixed with the formless (*arūpa*). "The formless" refers to pure formless [phenomena], because form is not included therein.
"By way of three each among the four aggregates" means that by way of grasping three each among the four aggregates, a self consisting of a mixture of form and formless is described;
in each such instance of grasping, there are formless phenomena distinct from feeling and the other [aggregates].
This is because all material phenomena are grasped together with the kasiṇa-form as a single unit.
Annihilationist views are taught in five instances, because one grasps those very same phenomena as "self" and because of their subsequent state of annihilation.
However, in the remaining fifteen instances, although the theorist grasps form as "self," they nevertheless perceive it there as permanent.
It does not abandon [the object] by means of the *kasiṇa* form, because it does not see the arising and so forth of that [form] mixed with it;
therefore, even there, the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) exists for him by way of grasping at partial eternity. It is an obstruction to the Path because it is a perverted view.

It is not an obstruction to heaven because it has not reached the level of a course of action (*akammapatha*). For only the views of non-action, causelessness, and nihilism are considered courses of action.

"Body" (*kāya*) refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*). It is indeed afflicted because its very nature consists of the taints (*āsava*). "Accompanied by lust, hatred, and delusion" means occurring within a mental continuum where lust, hatred, and delusion have not been abandoned.

"Here" means in this discourse. It is shown by way of its state of affliction. "By virtue of being free from defilements" means by virtue of having entered a mental continuum in which defilements have been personally abandoned.

Learners (*sekha*) do not have afflicted minds with respect to defilements already abandoned; however, they have afflicted minds with respect to those not yet abandoned. [The Buddhas] possess only non-afflicted minds.
They do not partake [of suffering] like the great masses who follow the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), because their minds lack the state of affliction due to the defilements (*kilesa*).
The commentary on the Nakulapitṛsūtra is finished.
2. Commentary on the Devadahasutta.
2. Kings are called "devas" because they "shine" (divyanti), meaning they sport, play, and dally with the strands of sensual pleasure, or because they "radiate" by the power of their own merit.
A conflagration among them is a "devadaha. Alternatively, it may have arisen spontaneously;
for that reason as well, it is called a "devadaha. The market town not far from it came to be designated simply as "Devadaha," just as [cities are named] "Varaṇanagara" or "Godhāgāma."
The western region (*pacchābhūma*) is the country situated in the western direction; those wishing to go there are "those going to the western region" (*pacchābhūmagamikā*).
"He made them share the burden" means he wished to make those monks share the burden by way of the elder.
If the elder was their burden, they were also his burden; thus it is said, "wishing to make them share the burden. For in this way, the elder [could] instruct them.
"He thinks [himself] one who should be instructed. Now, explaining this meaning, he says "For whoever," and so forth.
This is called "unburdened" because it does not proceed by taking any person as its own burden.

"In four ways" means: skill in the elements (*dhātu-kosalla*), skill in the sense-bases (*āyatana-kosalla*), skill in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-kosalla*), and skill in what is possible and impossible (*ṭhānāṭhāna-kosalla*)—thus in these four ways.
Taking along those who were elderly, afflicted by illness, or very young, he would go; for they were indeed free from fatigue after only two days.
Having related the story concerning the elephant, the horse, and the partridge, some say: "In Eḷakāḷagumba" means "in a bower of black grass thickets.

*Virajja* is sovereignty (*rajja*) that is manifold and various; *verajja* is simply that which is devoid of sovereignty (*virajja*), and that which has gone there is "gone to another country" (*paradesagata*).

This is the meaning. Therefore he said, “of one,” and so forth. “Cittasudatta and others” refers to the householder Citta, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others. “Inquirers” means those who investigate the Dhamma. “What? means of what kind.
“View” refers to the established doctrine (siddhanta). The intention is: he explains what it is like.
“Of the Dhamma” means of the Dhamma spoken by the Blessed One. “In accordance with the Dhamma” (anudhamma) means conformable, a principle that is non-contradictory. That...
However, he said, "the further explanation of what has been stated," referring to the expansion of the teaching according to the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
He said, "one who possesses the Dhamma is one who possesses the reason," because the Dhamma bears its own fruit; thus, it is a cause.
By this alternative reading as well, only the debate is indicated, not the action manifested by it.
The meaning of all six terms should be understood by way of craving (*taṇhā*) alone, because lust and the other [defilements] are merely specific states of craving.
Therefore he said, "Craving indeed," and so forth. It is called *vighāta* (affliction) because it afflicts both body and mind; thus he said, "Non-affliction means free from suffering.
It is called *upāyāsa* (despair) because it causes torment; that is, affliction. Its opposite, however, is *anupāyāsa* (non-despair).
The absence of fever should be observed. "In all cases" means in all sections.
The commentary on the Devadaha Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta.
3. Regarding the phrase “in Avantī and the Southern Road,” since this has appeared in other sections of the Sutta, he says “designated as Avantī and the Southern Road.
For the kingdom of Avantī lies to the south of the Middle Country. Because the doctrine (laddhi) was promulgated (*pavatta*) there, it is called “promulgated” (*pavatta*);
thus he says “the place where the doctrine was promulgated” (*laddhipavattaṭṭhāna*). Having established that a phenomenon (*dhamma*) is by nature subject to transformation (*ruppana-sabhāva*),...
The "form element" (rūpadhātu) refers to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha).

Kamma-consciousness is bound and fettered within the form element by means of lust—which serves as an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), whether co-nascent (sahajāta) or not co-nascent—as well as by means of its state of being unabandoned, which serves as a decisive support-condition (upanissayapaccaya).
It is called "wandering in its abode" (okasārī), because it is understood that it "wanders and proceeds in that abode known as the form element. It protects (avati).
It is called *oka* because one goes there and moves within it; it is a place of occurrence. Thus he said:

"one who has a home in the household, one who has a home in attachment. Alternatively, it is called *oka* because one enters into it and becomes unified with it through feeling and so forth; it refers to the eye, visible forms, and so on.

It is a condition by way of being an object and so forth. It is a condition both as immediate (*anantara*) and contiguous (*samanantara*), as well as by way of kamma, decisive support (*upanissaya*), object, and so forth.
When it was said, “The consciousness element, householder,” there might arise confusion as to which of the two—kamma-consciousness or resultant-consciousness—it refers to.
For the purpose of dispelling that confusion and for the purpose of its removal, the teaching was given as unmixed.
By way of object, the four stations of consciousness consisting of volitional formations were stated.
—“Or, bhikkhus, consciousness might persist by persisting with form as its support (*rūpupaya*), having form as its object,” and so forth.
This is also to show those stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).
They are called *upaya* because they approach their objects through the force of firm adherence; these are craving and views. They are the bases of such adherence.

They are the basis. They are the state of misapprehension (*abhinivesa*): they are the cause for proceeding by way of clinging to and adhering to this or that object. They are the state of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*):
they consist of the underlying tendency of lust (*rāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*). "At the upper limit" means at the upper limit of abandonment;
for it is only in the Buddhas that these are abandoned along with their latent dispositions (*savāsanā*). Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) not previously grasped remains ungrasped.
Having done so, he challenges why the teaching is given here: “Why is consciousness included here?

Previously, when it was stated that “consciousness is bound by craving for the consciousness-element,” there might have been confusion because the distinction between the condition and the conditioned is difficult to discern;
however, here there is no room for such confusion, as it refers generally to the abandoning of defilements in relation to all five aggregates.

Therefore he said, “For the purpose of showing the abandoning of the defilements,” and so forth. In the phrase “by kamma-consciousness not seeking an abode,” the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). “Not seeking” means not approaching.

“In the sense of a condition” means by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so on. “Sign” (*nimitta*) refers to that which causes arising. “Object... abode” (*niketa*): since form itself is the abode in the sense of being the place of dwelling designated as the making of an object, it is called “the sign of form as an abode” (*rūpanimittaniketa*).
“Because of the strength or weakness of desire and lust”: because of the powerful state of desire and lust toward the five internal aggregates, they are called “home”;
because of its weak state toward the six external objects, those are called “abode.
Now, in order to make the aforementioned meaning clear, it is said: “Even though...,” etc. It is called “home” (oka).

The "home" (*geha*) is so called because it is a place for staying at night; the "dwelling" (*niketa*) is so called because it is a place for staying during the day, such as a garden and so forth. Consequently, sensual desire (*chanda-rāga*) becomes weaker there.

"By the happiness based on the home" means that one is made happy, having attained happiness, through the mental pleasure derived from dependence on the home. "In matters to be done" refers to tasks both small and great that ought to be performed. "Himself" means by himself. "Within" refers to the inclination of the mind.

"Of such a kind" means of this particular form. The word *rūpa* (form) is like the word *vaṇṇa* (color); just as the word *rūpa* denotes the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it also denotes shape.

With the intention of explaining the meaning, it is said: "in forms such as long, short, black, white, and so forth. Regarding "in pleasure and so forth," this refers to mental joy (*somanassa*) and the rest;
for therein there might be the aspiration, "May I frequently experience mental joy. "One who has such perception" expresses an aspiration for a specific kind of perception by way of its object.
"One who has such consciousness," however, here expresses an aspiration for a specific kind of consciousness by way of its object.
He says: “May my consciousness be capable of perceiving forms so exquisite, and may it have as its support a body adorned with such fivefold clarity.
“Not making a circle before him” means not aspiring for anything in the world. “Unpolished” means that what precedes and follows is unconnected.
It is called a "dispute" (*vāda*) because they dispute by means of it; thus he said, "It is your fault," and so forth. "Right here" (*idheva*) means in this very assembly.
"Clear yourself" (*nibbeṭhehi*) means free yourself from the fault.
The commentary on the Hāliddikāni Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second Hāliddikāni Sutta.
"In the Cūḷachakkapañha" refers to the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa. "In the Mahāsakkapañha" also refers to the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.
"This" refers to the sūtra passage beginning with "those recluses and brahmins. It is called *taṇhāsaṅkhaya* because craving (*taṇhā*) is completely exhausted (*sammadeva khīyati*) therein.
He said, "in the unconditioned element," meaning "in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of craving. "Those who have transcended the ultimate goal" means those for whom the goal has vanished.
Therefore he said, "those whose goal is constant. "In the remaining phrases" refers to such passages as "those who have attained absolute security" and so forth.
The commentary on the second Hāliddikāni Sutta is finished.

5. Commentary on the Samādhi Sutta “Concentration” (samādhi) refers either to absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). “Meditation subject” (kammaṭṭhāna) refers to the meditation subject for insight (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) which has concentration as its basis.
The reading is “it will expand” (phātiṃ gamissati). “He aspires” means: “O, may such a form as this be mine! “He declares” means...

He speaks of "adherence" (abhinivesa) by way of craving and views. Therefore he said, "by means of that delight," and so forth. Even when there is no verbal expression such as "O, how dear! How desirable!
if there is the arising of greed in that manner, one is indeed said to "assert" (abhivadati). Therefore he said, "without breaking his speech.
Grasping while appropriating it for oneself as "this is mine," making it as if it were not the domain of anything else;
Showing that one "remains attached" (ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati), he said: "Having swallowed means having finalized [the object], one grasps it.
Phrases such as "one delights in" (abhinandati) are stated with reference to the preliminary stage, whereas "delight arises" (uppajjati nandī) refers to the moment of arrival at the sense-door.

Some maintain that the former terms refer to the underlying tendency (anusaya) and the latter to the active obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna), while others take "clinging" (upādāna) in the sense of grasping. One neither delights in nor speaks in praise of it.
Here, the meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated above. “He does not say ‘desired’ or ‘loved’” means he does not say it is “desired,” nor does he say it is “loved.
He does not even speak of it because of the absence of clinging through craving.
The commentary on the Samādhi Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Paṭisallāṇa Sutta.

He said this "having known" [it] because he knew: "When there is physical seclusion, there is mental seclusion; when that exists, it is fitting to obtain seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka) as well.
The commentary on the Paṭisallāṇa Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Agitation through Clinging (Upādāparitassanāsutta) “Agitation arising from grasping”:
this refers to the agitation of craving (*taṇhā-paritassanā*) and the agitation of views (*diṭṭhi-paritassanā*) that arise within the five aggregates through the grasping [of them] as “I” and “mine.
“Non-agitation” (*aparitassanā*): this means the absence of agitation, the opposite of agitation.
Or: "Alas, this strength and youth! refers to consciousness as kamma-viññāṇa—that is, consciousness accompanied by craving and views which has change as its object, along with that which follows it.
"Anuparivatti" (revolving) means occurring by taking that [change] as its object. Therefore he said: "from the mind that has change as its object.
"The arising of unwholesome states" refers to the arising of other unwholesome states through craving. "Having exhausted" means having consumed.
Without giving it the opportunity to proceed: "With anxiety" means with anxiety by way of craving and views.
"Having grasped" means having been seized by the graspings of craving and views, and thus being agitated by them. "The mind does not follow after the breaking up of form.
"It is fitting" means it is appropriate to speak in every respect.
The commentary on the *Upādāparitassanā-sutta* is finished.
8. The commentary on the second *Upādāparitassanā-sutta*.

The teaching was given by way of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*), because it is introduced with the teaching: “This is mine, this I am, this is my self. “In the four suttas” means in the four suttas beginning with the fifth. However, in the fourth [sutta], only the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is discussed.
The commentary on the second Discourse on Agitation through Clinging is finished.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Impermanence in the Three Times:
If the past and the future are impermanent because they do not exist at present, then the present must also not exist at that time.
What need is there to speak of its impermanence? What talk can there be regarding the present, since it is delimited by arising and passing away?
For this has been said: "Those things that have arisen and persist are like mustard seeds on the point of an awl.
The commentary on the Sutta on the Impermanence of the Three Times is concluded.
10–11. Commentary on the Sutta on Suffering in the Three Times, etc. 10–11.
"In exactly that same manner" means: just as the ninth sutta was spoken according to the specific disposition of the individuals [addressed], so too [was this one spoken].
It is said that those bhikkhus perceived the past and the future as "suffering," and likewise perceived them as "non-self."
In the present, they grew weary. "Then for them," and so forth—all should be stated according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the Sutta on the Suffering of the Three Times and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Nakulapituvagga is concluded.
2. Aniccavagga (The Chapter on Impermanence) 1–10. Commentary on the Discourses on Impermanence, etc. 12–21.
*Pucchāvasika* (Dependent on Questions): Because these were taught by way of the questions of the Elder Ānanda.
The commentary on the *Anicca-sutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Anicca-vagga* is finished.
3. The *Bhāra-vagga*.
1. Commentary on the Bhārasutta 22.
The aggregates that have become the objects of clinging are the "aggregates subject to clinging" (*upādānakkhandhā*).

"In the sense of being heavy to carry" means by way of the state of being heavy to carry, by way of their greater weight. To make the meaning already stated clear, he said: "For of these... and so forth.

In this context, because these activities such as standing, walking, and so forth succeed through mutual dependence—like a cripple and a person blind from birth—and not individually, the term "of these" is used without distinction. By "person," he refers to the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha-santāna*).
For the continuity of the aggregates, proceeding without interruption until final Nibbāna, carries the burden of the aggregates.
It appears as if carrying [the burden] in the world, because there is no being apart from that [process]. Therefore he said, "The person," and so forth.
"Born as a bearer of the burden" means one who has become known as a bearer of the burden.

"Leading to renewed existence" (*ponobhavika*): renewed existence (*punabbhava*) is the making of renewed existence; it either deserves that fruit, or it is connected to it. Thus it is "leading to renewed existence."
"Accompanied by that state" means, for example, "phenomena that are visible"; it does not mean accompanied by association, nor does it mean accompanied by an object.
"In this or that place" refers to whichever place of rebirth, or having reached an object such as form, one finds delight therein.

Therefore he said, "or in a place of rebirth," and so forth. "Consisting of the five strands of sensual pleasure" means having the five strands of sensual pleasure as its object. [This occurs] in the fine-material and immaterial realms of rebirth.
Attachment is attachment to existence in the realms of form and formlessness. Craving for meditative absorption is attachment to the kamma-existence known as jhāna.

"Eternalist views," etc., refers to the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*); the attachment associated with that is called craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*). The view of annihilation is called the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*);
the desire and attachment associated with that is called craving for non-existence (*vibhava-taṇhā*). This person thus takes up the burden of the aggregates.

Because rebirth-linking is grasped by way of craving, all such phrases as "herein craving is detached from without remainder, it fades away, ceases, and is abandoned" should be understood solely in reference to Nibbāna; thus he said, "all are synonyms for Nibbāna alone.
The commentary on the Bhāra Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Pariññāsutta 23.

“To be fully understood” (*parijānitabba*) means to be fully understood by means of the full understanding of abandonment (*pahānapariññā*). And such full understanding therein is the abandoning of desire and lust, as well as the transcending of them;
thus he says, “the meaning is ‘to be transcended. He speaks of Nibbāna as “ultimate full understanding” (*accantapariññā*).
Therefore he said, "They transcend; this is the meaning.
The commentary on the Pariññā Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Abhiññā Sutta.

24. Full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) is spoken of by taking it to mean "knowing with distinguished wisdom. By the second phrase means by the phrase "fully understanding" (*parijānan*). By the third and fourth [phrases] means by the phrases "fading away" (*virājayam*) and "abandoning" (*pajaham*).
The commentary on the *Abhiññā-sutta* is finished.
4–9. Commentary on the *Chandarāga-sutta* and others.

25–30. These should be understood in the same manner as explained in the *Dhātusaṃyutta*; for here the teaching is presented solely by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), whereas there it was by way of the elements (*dhātu*)—this is the only difference.
The four truths are spoken of because the teaching proceeds by way of gratification (*assāda*), danger (*ādīnava*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*).
The commentary on the Chandarāgasutta and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the Aghamūlasutta:
31. "Agha" is said to mean evil; because it is the cause of evil, suffering (dukkha) is called "agha. For this so-called suffering is, in particular—
It is caused by evil and designated as the fruit of karma. Likewise, the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) has its root in ignorance and craving.

Because it is the cause of misfortune (*agha*), it is "misfortune," that is, suffering. For the great mass of people who follow the round of existence, being overwhelmed by suffering, perform various actions while imagining them to be a remedy for it.
The commentary on the Aghamūla Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Pabhaṅgu Sutta:
"Of a nature to break up" means having a nature that breaks up moment by moment.
The commentary on the Pabhaṅgu Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Bhāravagga is finished.
4. The Natumhākavagga.
1. Commentary on the *Natumhākaṃ-sutta* 33.
"By the abandoning of desire and lust" means by the relinquishing of the desire and lust connected thereto. Grass such as *dabba* and so forth is already well known;

therefore, palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth are mentioned in order to show what is not well known, or for the purpose of showing the distinction between grasses and wood. *Piyāla* is *phārusaka*.
The commentary on the *Natumhākaṃ-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Aññatarabhikkhu-sutta* 35.
"If it underlies form" means: if lust and the other [defilements] arise with respect to form-phenomena by way of underlying tendency (*anusaya*).
“It is reckoned by that” means that by means of that lust and so forth, the person possessing it comes to be designated—i.e., to be conventionally expressed—as “lustful,” “hateful,” and so on.
Therefore he said, “In the case of sensual lust, etc. “By what is unreal” means by what is unborn, not occurring by way of latent tendency (*anusaya*).
Here, he speaks of “overpowering” by way of the head-term *anusaya*. Hence [it is said]: “reckoned as ‘lustful,’ ‘hateful,’ or ‘deluded’...”
"It does not go," it is said. For, in the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*), the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) are those defilements that are to be abandoned by the Path.
The commentary on the *Aññatarabhikkhu-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second *Aññatarabhikkhu-sutta*.
36. "That form which is underlain" means that the form underlain by lust and so forth follows along with the underlying tendency (anusaya) at the time of death.
Therefore it is said, "Indeed not," and so on. By whichever underlying tendency one dies, one follows along with that;

because of being characterized by that, one receives such designations as "one who is lustful" and so forth. It is by means of whichever underlying tendency acting as the cause that one is inferred. By that [cause].
The commentary on the second *Aññatarabhikkhu-sutta* is concluded.
5–6. Commentary on the *Ānanda-sutta*, etc., 37–38.

"Stability" (*ṭhiti*) means that which is accompanied by the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). "Alteration of what is stable" (*ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ*) refers to [the moment] after the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*).
“Becoming otherwise” (*aññathābhāvo*). “Is manifested” (*paññāyati*) means it is apprehended.

Because it exists by way of conditions, aging is manifested through the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of one who is living, due to reaching a state of alteration from the moment of arising. To make the meaning already stated more clear, it was said:
“Stability,” and so forth. [The phrase] “life... [and so on] refers to the name. For thus it is said in the Abhidhamma: “Life is stability.”
It has been explained. "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) is to be connected with "of aging" (*jarāya*).
There are three characteristics by way of the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-sabhāva-lakkhaṇa*).

Whatever conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) there may be—whether material or immaterial, mundane or supramundane—it is a conditioned phenomenon, not a characteristic, because its intrinsic nature consists of arising and so forth. [The others] are characteristics.

A conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) does not [exist] because it is devoid of arising and so forth. Nor... [omission] ...is it possible [to know it] as a conditioned phenomenon without its characteristic, because it is a conditioned thing.
Nor can a conditioned phenomenon be made known by way of its nature as a conditioned phenomenon without its characteristic. Therefore he said, "by means of the characteristic," and so forth.

Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned meaning by means of a simile, he said, "Just as," and so forth. Therein, "characteristic" refers to the characteristic of the state of being black, red, variegated, and so on.
It becomes evident that "this is such-and-such a cow.
In the same way, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) are also discerned by one who investigates them according to their intrinsic nature;

for the characteristic of arising is treated as the state of arising. "Designated by time" means designated by the time of its arising. "Of that conditioned phenomenon": even the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa).
It is discerned. "Arising" (*uppāda*) means the characteristic of arising (*uppāda-lakkhaṇa*). The "characteristic of aging" (*jarā-lakkhaṇa*) is the characteristic of the aging of what has arisen;

that is stated as "the alteration of what is present" (*ṭhitassa aññathatta*). The reading is: "At the moment of dissolution, both the formation (*saṅkhāra*) and its characteristic, which is reckoned as time, and even its moment (*khaṇa*), are discerned. However, some insert the word "aging" (*jarā*) here as well. And thus—
They say: "At that moment, a formation does not break up while being young;
rather, it breaks up only after having become old, like an aged person. Their intention is that aging is overcome by breaking up itself;
because the moment is so extremely brief, it cannot be designated as "stability. "Those" refers to the three characteristics of immaterial phenomena.
"At the moment of existence" (atthikkhaṇa) means the moment when immaterial phenomena are present; the intention is "the moment of arising" (uppādakkhaṇa).
"Of all phenomena" (sabbadhammānaṃ) means that for all material and immaterial phenomena, there can be no duration (ṭhiti). "Of that very [phenomenon]" (tasseva) means of that very duration.
"That meaning" (tam atthaṃ) refers to the state of being impossible to point out the characteristic of aging (jarā). Others, however, say: "Duration is staying by way of continuity."
They say this, but that is without cause and without foundation. For in the Sutta, it is said:

"The alteration of what stands is discerned," because stability is shown as being indistinguishable from arising and passing away. As for what ought to be said here, that has already been stated above.
Furthermore, just as the state of dissolution is held to be distinct from the state of the phenomenon's arising, otherwise [if they were identical], that which is arising itself...
One falls into the position that [the dhamma] "breaks up"; thus, even at the stage of dissolution, a stage facing dissolution must be admitted as distinct from the stage of dissolution itself.
For that which is not facing dissolution does not break up. Nor can one here imagine a stage facing arising, because at that time it has not yet attained its acquisition of existence.
This is the distinction: the so-called moment of stability belongs to material phenomena alone.
"Nor non-material phenomena"—this is such a distinction. "The teacher's opinion" means the opinion of that very teacher;
since it is the weakest of all, he said "therefore," and so forth.
The commentary on the Ānanda-sutta and others is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the *Anudhammasutta*, etc. (39–42).

Because it holds one back from falling into the suffering of the states of deprivation (*apāya*) and the suffering of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the Dhamma consists of the path, the fruition, and Nibbāna.

And because the preliminary practice leading up to that is in conformity with it, he says, “of one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma,” and so forth. “Abounding in disenchantment (*nibbidā*): [End of section]

In the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the word extraction (*paduddhāra*) has been made; however, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is stated: "One should dwell with a mind full of disenchantment" (*nibbidābahulaṃ vihareyya*).

"Full of disenchantment" (*ukkaṇṭhanabahulo*) means one who is full of disenchantment toward all states of existence (*sabbabhava*). "By the three kinds of full understanding" (*tīhi pariññāhi*) refers to the full understandings of knowing (*ñāta*), scrutinizing (*tīraṇa*), and abandoning (*pahāna*).

"He fully understands" (*parijānāti*) means he knows by discerning the phenomena of the three planes (*tebhūmakadhamma*), and thus he brings insight meditation (*vipassanā*) to its peak. He is completely liberated (*parimuccati*).

Because it is stated that "the path proceeds as being liberated from all defilements. By the word "likewise" (tathā), he indicates that in the three [subsequent] cases following this one, there is a path.

"Here" (idha) means in this discourse. "Unspecified" (aniyamitā) means not taken up. Among those, they are "specified" because of the statement beginning with "contemplating impermanence" (aniccānupassī).
"That" refers to the contemplation (anupassanā). In that context, the phrase "precisely by way of being specified" is a statement regarding its characteristic (lakkhaṇa).

"Just as one might say, 'If I were to have diseases, this medicine should be given,'" so too it is not possible to bring the practice of comprehension to its ultimate perfection by means of this contemplation alone.
The commentary on the *Anudhammasutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Chapter on Your Own Group is finished.
5. The Chapter on Being an Island to Oneself. 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Being an Island to Oneself.
43. It is an island (*dīpa*) because water has gone away from it in two ways; or it is an island because it is like an island, in the sense of being unassailable by floods.

That which is not another is the self (*attā*); however, in this context, "dhamma" is intended. Those for whom the self is an island are "self-islands. Since the meaning of "island" is that of a refuge, he said:
"‘Having the self as refuge’ is a synonym for that very same thing. This pertains to both the mundane and the supramundane.

The Dhamma is called "self" because it is the absolute protector. It is said that "the meaning stated by the first word is stated by the second word as well," which is why he says, "Therefore he said...
and so forth. That from which a fruit is produced is a *yoni*, meaning a cause.
"Of what origin" (*kiṃ-pabhutika*) means: what is their source of arising? This was undertaken for the purpose of showing [their] abandonment. Therefore he said:
“Both formerly... [as before] ... they are abandoned. He does not tremble because of the absence of the trembling of craving (*taṇhā-paritāsa*).
“By means of the factor of insight” means by means of the cause designated as insight (*vipassanā*).
The commentary on the *Attadīpa Sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Paṭipadā-sutta* 44.

Because it exists as a real entity by its own nature (*sabhāvato*), the body—which is a collection of phenomena such as form and so forth—is called "personality" (*sakkāya*). Thus it is said: "Personality is suffering.
"View" (*diṭṭhi*) itself is "regard" (*samanupassanā*); or, regard accompanied by view is "view-regard" (*diṭṭhisamanupassanā*). [This refers to] the conceiving of a self through views.

Together with the other conceivings. Together with insight, the knowledge of the four paths is "clear vision" (*samanupassanā*), because it is made to be "the seeing of the four noble truths correctly and appropriately.
The commentary on the *Paṭipadā-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the Aniccasutta 45.
"Dispassion" (virāga) is the path, and "liberation" (vimutti) is the fruit; thus it is said: "One becomes dispassionate at the moment of the path, and one is liberated at the moment of the fruit.
"Without grasping" means that while the taints (āsava) are thus ceasing, one does not grasp at any phenomenon as "I" or "mine."
Because it is said, "The mind is dispassionate, it is liberated," the fruit is grasped; because it is said, "Birth is exhausted," and so forth, there is reviewing.
Thus he says, "together with the fruit, for the purpose of showing reviewing. It stands because there is no further duty to be performed.
Therefore he says, "standing because of being liberated. That which was to be attained has been attained through the attainment of the supreme fruit.
Content and thoroughly satisfied because of having attained [this realization].
The commentary on the *Anicca-sutta* is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second *Anicca-sutta*.

46. "The past" (*pubbanta*) refers to the portion consisting of the aggregates of the past. "Followed" (*anugatā*) means followed by way of grasping after formulating [views] such as eternalism and so forth.

"The eighteen views" (*aṭṭhārasa diṭṭhiyo*) are: four views of eternalism, four views of partial eternalism, four views of finitude and infinity, four views of evasion through sophistry (*amarāvikkhepa*), and two views of fortuitous origination.

Thus, by the destruction of conditions, these eighteen views do not exist. They follow along with the grasping that conceives of the future portion of the aggregates—*aparanta*—as having such states as eternalism and so forth.

These consist of: sixteen theories of percipient existence (*saññīvāda*), eight theories of non-percipient existence (*asaññīvāda*), eight theories of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence (*nevasaññīnāsaññīvāda*), seven theories of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), and five theories of Nibbāna in the present life (*paramadiṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*).

Thus, by the destruction of conditions, these forty-four views do not exist; neither the obsession with the view of eternalism nor the misapprehension of rules and observances exists by the destruction of conditions.
Therefore he said, "To this extent the first path is shown," because of the description of the abandonment of all views without exception.
They are abandoned and suppressed. But this [passage], beginning with "In form," etc., is as follows:
The commentary on the Second Anicca Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Samanupassanā Sutta: 47.
"By way of grasping [them] as a whole" means by way of grasping the five aggregates collectively and without exception as "self."
They regard one or another of these five aggregates of clinging as "self. "Thus" (iti) means in this way.
For whatever person this view of self—termed "regarding"—exists, it is found because it has not been struck down by its opposite.
"Of the five faculties" refers to the faculties beginning with the eye.
"Object" means the object of kamma-consciousness. Since the grasping "I am" arises by way of conceit and by way of views, the craving associated with that [grasping] is also included therein;
thus it is said: "By way of craving, conceit, and views, 'I am' occurs for him in this manner.
"Having grasped" means having grasped by way of the basis for the notion of "I. "This is I": this refers to the eye and so forth.

Or [the view] "I am possessed of pleasure," and so forth. Because it proceeds by way of grasping such things as "the self is material and free from disease after death," it is said that "all [views] such as 'they will be material' belong exclusively to eternalism.

Prior to the fixation upon insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*), the five faculties exist in their respective modes; likewise, subsequent to the fixation upon insight, while they remain in those very same modes—
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is abandoned regarding the faculties such as the eye by developing insight (*vipassanā*) and thereby giving rise to the Path (*magga*).

Then, through the succession of paths, the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (*arahattamagga-vijjā*) arises. Craving, conceit, and views [are abandoned] because they constitute the accumulation of kamma.
Regarding "one link of kamma" ... [etc. ... "one link": this refers to the link between cause and fruit. Again, "one link": this speaks of the link between fruit and cause.
The three kinds of conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) refer to the past time, because it is the time of past existence that is intended here.

The condition for the future has been shown by way of the uninstructed worldling (*puthujjana*); however, by way of the instructed noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*), the stilling of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) is shown.
The commentary on the *Samanupassanā-sutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Khandha Sutta 48.

"In the same way" means precisely by way of being an object (*ārammaṇa*). That which is to be grasped (*upādātabba*) by means of clinging (*upādāna*) through the act of making an object is "clinging-favorable" (*upādāniya*). "Here too" refers even to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
If it were taken in the sense of analysis (*vibhāga*), there might also be the undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭha-pasaṅga*) [of over-extension] in the Abhidhamma.
And because of the statement, "having gathered them together into a single mass," it is said specifically "in the sense of a mass" (*rāsaṭṭhena*).
The commentary on the *Khandhasutta* is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the *Soṇasutta*, etc.
49–50. *Visiṭṭha* means preeminent. *Uttama* means supreme. "What else could there be?"—what other reason could there be?
This is because, through such a mode of contemplation, others are found to be non-existent due to the breaking down of verbal designations.
The teaching known as the "Splitting of the Thunderbolt" (*vajirabhedadesanā*) is, in its meaning, a threefold-turning teaching (*teparivaṭṭadesanā*).
The commentary on the Soṇasutta and others is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Nandikkhayasutta and others: 51–52.
Regarding the phrase "in the ninth and tenth," these two suttas are cited together because their commentaries on the meaning are similar.

In the sense of delighting, it is *nandī*; in the sense of coloring, it is *rāga*. Although there is a difference in their lexical meanings (*saddattha*), it was stated that "there is no distinction between them in meaning";
nevertheless, it is shown that a mere distinction can still be found by way of the difference between the states that abandon [them].
Thus, the passage beginning with "or by means of the contemplation of disenchantment" was spoken. The connection is: "one who becomes dispassionate abandons lust. "To this extent" means:
“With the destruction of delight comes the destruction of lust”—this much [is said]. Having brought insight (vipassanā) to its conclusion, it is by means of the completion of the function of insight.
“Destruction of lust” is so called because lust has been exhausted by the insight that culminates in emergence.
“Destruction of delight” occurs by way of total eradication through the Noble Path that arises immediately thereafter. Therefore he said: “Having shown the path here.”

Immediately thereafter, however, by means of the noble fruit that has arisen, through the subsiding [of defilements], the mind is liberated from all defilement due to the destruction of delight and lust. Therefore he said, "The fruit has been shown.
The commentary on the *Nandikkhaya-sutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Attadīpa-vagga is finished.
The Mūlapaṇṇāsaka is complete.
6. The Upaya-vagga.
1. Commentary on the *Upāyasutta* 53.
It approaches (*upeti*), thus it is an approach (*upāya*). How does it approach? By way of craving, conceit, and so forth;
hence he says, “by way of craving, conceit, and views. How is this established? From the statement “not liberated. For one who is bound by way of craving and views—what does he approach?
He said, "The five aggregates," because there is no such thing as one who approaches [rebirth] apart from them. But who is it that approaches? It is the person possessing those [aggregates].
Since the act of approaching is stated here by way of craving and views, they say that "consciousness" refers specifically to unwholesome kamma-consciousness.
"Having made it impel" means having made it take on momentum; that is, having made it capable of drawing forth rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
Therefore he said, “Rebirth-linking,” and so forth. The reason for not mentioning [the object] was already stated in the commentary on the verse, “Having abandoned the home, wandering homeless.
By way of the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) and so on, the object that serves as the condition for rebirth-linking ceases by virtue of the karma that produces that rebirth-linking.
It does not become a foundation because it does not persist, as in the case when one is still possessed of lust. Thus it is “unestablished.”
Consciousness [is understood] in the manner already stated. "Without having conditioned" means without producing it, by way of destroying the conditions.
The commentary on the *Upaya-sutta* is finished.
2. Commentary on the *Bīja-sutta*.
54. Regarding the phrase "born from seeds" (*bījajātāni*), he says "seeds" (*bījāni*) because the word *jāta* is used merely for the sake of completing the meter.

*Vacā* is white sweet flag (*setavacaṃ*). *Ajjuka* is a woodcutter’s root (*tacchakaṃ*). *Phaṇijjaka* is *tulasi*. "Unbroken" means not damaged even in part. "For the purpose of seed" means for the function of a seed.
"It does not serve" shows that it is not a requisite condition (*paccaya*). "Not brought forth" means not putrid.

They have approached [the object]. They are "essence-seizers" (*sārādāni*) because they seize the essence of the grain-pith. They are "stations of consciousness" (*viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) because consciousness stands there by way of grasping an object.

"By way of object" means by way of being an objective state. "In the sense of moistening" means by way of craving, through the production of slickness; hence it is said that [craving] "is the sprinkling of delight. For in this way, that projected kamma-consciousness—

It is capable of producing the sprout of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "With conditions" means it is possessed of conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) and improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
It "grows," meaning it becomes capable of generating the continuum of karmic result (*vipāka-santāna*).
The commentary on the Seed Sutta is finished.
3. Udānasuttavaṇṇanā 55.
"He uttered an udāna" means he let out a cry of satisfaction. This is the aforementioned utterance. *Upanissaya* means a powerful support;
giving itself as the support is "giving-support" (*dānūpanissaya*). This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Therein, "giving-support" (refers to...)

It becomes "strong" by way of its strength, as in the case of food and other requisites; therefore, one who is rich in such decisive support (*upanissaya*) and has already cultivated familiarity through the abandoning of sensual lust attains the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) before long while applying himself to insight (*vipassanā*).
Likewise, one who has the well-purified virtue as decisive support [attains it] through the loathing of the defects of sense-desire. If this is so, why are these two considered decisive supports?

Why is it called "weak"? Because it serves as a condition only for knowledge that is like lightning. Even that [knowledge] occurs only by obtaining the support of the development [of concentration], not by itself alone.
However, development is a powerful decisive support (upanissaya) because it is the specific cause for penetration.
For it is the specific condition for knowledge that is like a thunderbolt. Therefore, it is said: "The decisive support of development brings about Arahantship."
"He" refers to the Elder Milakatthera. "Vihāra" means a dwelling place; for the elder dwelt in a leaf-hut on the outskirts of the monastery.
He attends [to it] with a single characteristic, just as a bull accustomed to the peak attends the path of travel.
"Therein" means in the heap of wet firewood. "Of water-jars" means of water-vessels.
He applied [the teachings] to himself alone because the qualities spoken of in the *udāna* were found complete within him.

Therefore, he said, "By means of diligence," and so forth. For this Elder Milaka was established as one of purified virtue, fulfilling his duties and obligations with reverence for the training and great respect;
therefore, it was said, "with weak supporting conditions. Thus the Blessed One said.
He utters the *udāna*: “May I not be... [and so on] ...the fetters.
“If I were not to exist” means: if there were no such thing as someone denoted by the word “I,” because of the non-existence of any referent for that term;
and for that very reason, my requisites too would not exist, since they are subject to disintegration.

Because of its lack of stability. Having thus explained the meaning of the two phrases by way of referring to oneself, the passage beginning with "Or else" (*sace vā pana*) was spoken in order to explain it now by way of kamma and its fruit.

Having shown emptiness by way of the past and the present, the passage beginning with "But now" (*idāni pana*) was spoken to show that same [emptiness] by way of the present and the future. Thus he resolves.
While proceeding with such a resolution. "Vibhavissati" means it will perish; for *vibhava* is indeed destruction.
Therefore he said, "it will break up. He said, "by the vision of *vibhava*," because the term *vibhava-dassana* is stated by eliding the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
The vision of *vibhava* is the vision of absolute destruction. "That" refers to the Noble Path. This is a general designation.
"It is the culmination of distinction" (visesa-niṭṭhā) should be understood as meaning by way of the third path.
"The path and fruit above" refers to the fruit of the supreme path. "Immediate" (anantara) means there is no interval between this [insight] and birth;
thus insight is immediate to the path. However, because the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) is included within the sequence of conformity (anuloma), it either follows the course of insight or—
It might be argued that because it has Nibbāna as its object, it follows the same course as the Path; however, the Path does not thereby become something "intermediate. Therefore he said:

"Insight is called the immediate neighbor of the Path. But the Fruit, because it has Nibbāna as its object, because it functions by way of abandoning the defilements, and because it is supramundane, follows the same course as the wholesome Path; this is due to its being a wholesome resultant state.
However, since their purpose is their differentiation, it may be said that [the fruit] is immediately subsequent to insight; thus it is stated: "The fruit is called 'distantly immediate'.
But when "the destruction of the taints" is spoken of in reference to the supreme path, there is no need to mention the proximity of the insights.
*Atasitāye*: not to be feared, meaning not to be subjected to fear. *Tāso*: the cause of fear.
“*Tasati etasmā*”: having understood it thus. *So*: that unlearned worldling (*puthujjana*). *Tilakkhaṇāhaṭan* (struck by the three characteristics):

characterized by the three marks such as impermanence and so forth. *Manamhi naṭṭho*: I am slightly lost; the intention is that even beyond that, because he remains right there and has not fulfilled anything, he is [considered] liberated.
Having said, “There is no such thing as fear,” in order to show his state of being fearless, [he says] “na...”

"‘Hī’ and so forth was said. For a noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), while practicing insight (*vipassanā*) with the knowledge of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇa*) that ‘conditioned phenomena are fearful,’ does not tremble.
The commentary on the Udāna Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Upādānaparivaṭṭa Sutta* 56.
"By way of the four turnings" means by way of the turning of the Four Noble Truths within each individual aggregate (*khandha*).

"He fully understood form" means that he understood all derived and primary material form (*rūpa*) as being base due to its nature of corruption, and because of the emptiness and delusion inherent therein.
“I understood and penetrated [it] as ‘the noble truth of suffering’ through distinguished knowledge.
Because the decline, growth, and so forth of the material body are evident by way of nutriment, and because it is its specific condition, it is stated as “originating from nutriment.

Since the discourse on the origin of suffering is the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), it is stated specifically as “with desire and lust. By the inclusion of the terms “desire and lust,”...
And clinging, karma, and ignorance are indeed included as well; the meaning is that they are "practicing.
This is an expression in the present tense, just as in the phrase, "a wholesome consciousness has arisen. "They establish themselves" means they obtain a footing.

Regarding the term "those who are complete" (*kevalino*), he says here that completeness is due to the quality of liberation: "those who are whole, having performed all their duties. "By which they... [is the beginning of the next clause].

That by which they might designate them as "those beyond training" (asekha) through what remains [of their path] does not exist for them to be designated in the same way as for those still in training (sekha).

"Vatta" means a cause in the sense of being a process, and in the sense of the occurrence of the fruit. "The section on the plane of those beyond training" means the manifestation of the plane of those beyond training.
The commentary on the *Upādānaparipavatta-sutta* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Sattaṭṭhāna-sutta* 57.
“In seven places” means in the seven areas beginning with the understanding of form (*rūpa*). “One who has lived the life” means one who has lived the noble life (*ariyavāsa*).
"In this" means in this enumeration. "The rest" refers to what remains after that which has been stated here. "In the manner stated" should be understood according to the method explained below.
"Delight in excellence" (*ussadanandi*) is the gladdening and cheering of one who possesses abundant virtues;

it is that which entices through the praise of virtues by producing confidence in those still in training (*sekkha*) and in noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*). Now, the very meaning just stated will be made clear.
The passage beginning with “Just as” (*yathā hi*) was stated in order to explain how [this can be done].
“By this much” means by this sequence of teaching, which demonstrates proficiency in seven points by way of the five aggregates.
“That” refers to the object. “Merely the elements and so forth” means merely the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). In these...
“In phenomena” means in these [categories] beginning with birth. “Having performed the work” means having completed the work of comprehension (*sammasana*).

Thus, having analyzed here the occurrence of skill in the seven bases by way of the five aggregates through their various divisions, the King of Dhamma shows that it is “a threefold close investigation.
The commentary on the Sutta of the Seven Bases is concluded.
6. Commentary on the *Sammāsambuddhasutta* 58.

That by which one directs (*payasati*) or applies oneself with excess (*adhika*) and distinction (*visesa*) is *adhippāyo*, meaning distinguished application. Therefore, he says, “excessive application.
By the phrase “this path,” he refers to the Noble Eightfold Path. “Here” means in this discourse.
"In the sense of not being currently occurring" means in the state of not being present prior to the arising of a Buddha.
"He knows the path" means he knows and understands the noble path together with its preliminary stages, its requisites, its domain, its fruit, and its outcome; thus, he is "one who knows the path.
"Known" means it is known and attained by others as well, like an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand.
He made it manifest as if it were before his eyes, and having done so, he taught it.

Since one practices on the path by avoiding what is not the path, just as skill in the path is required, so too must skill regarding what is not the path be desired; thus he said, "skilled in both the path and the non-path.
"I have gone first" means that I am endowed with the foremost path.
The commentary on the *Sammāsambuddhasutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Anattalakkhaṇasutta* 59.
"Former attendants" (*purāṇupaṭṭhāke*) means those who were attendants during the previous time of striving and exertion. [He said this] in the sense of their lack of mastery (*avasavattanaṭṭhena*).
“By way of being ownerless, by way of emptiness, and by way of the negation of a self”—thus [it is] by means of those [criteria] stated previously.
“By this much of a passage” means by this portion of the sutta beginning with “Bhikkhus, form is non-self” and extending as far as “Let my consciousness not be thus.
An answer is the speaking of what has not yet been said, not of what has already been said; thus it was said: “Those...”
"Having shown," means having brought together. "Detailed exposition" (*vitthārakathā*) means the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in its full detail.

It is stated as "the characteristic of non-self alone" because of the predominance and primary importance of that [characteristic] therein. For even impermanence and the other [characteristics] are mentioned there solely for the purpose of illuminating that [non-self];
thus, that alone is the foremost and the primary, both due to its nature and because of the inclination of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
The commentary on the *Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* is finished.
8. Commentary on the *Mahāli Sutta*. 60.
The phrases beginning with "entirely suffering" (*ekantadukkha*) follow the same method as previously stated; therefore, their meaning should be understood according to the method explained therein.
And here, it should be understood that just as lust is the cause and condition for defilement, so too is the path accompanied by insight the cause and condition for purification.
The commentary on the Mahāli Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Āditta Sutta 61.

“By eleven” means by the eleven fires, beginning with lust (*rāga*) and ending with despair (*upāyāsa*), in the sense of being a source of torment. “In two” refers to the eighth and ninth [fires]. “Only the characteristic of suffering” is stated because of the abundance of that [suffering] and because it is predominant therein.
The commentary on the Āditta Sutta is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Niruttipathasutta* 62.

"The paths of language" (*niruttipatha*) refers to linguistic expressions themselves; by the word "path" (*patha*), he indicates an extension of the term, as in the expression, "seeds themselves are the classes of seeds. "By way of etymology" (*niruttivasena*) means by way of derivation (*nibbacana*).

And they are "paths" because they exist in accordance with their respective meanings. "All three" refers to the terms for language (*nirutti*), designation (*adhivacana*), and description (*paññatti*).
For instance, a term such as “contact (phassa) is so called because it touches” is *nirutti* (etymological derivation), having been extracted [from its root].

A term such as “Sirīvaḍḍhaka” or “Dhanavaḍḍhaka” is *adhivacana* (designation), occurring by taking the mere verbal expression as its basis.
