A term such as “reasoning (takka) is initial application (vitakka)” is *paññatti* (conceptual description), because it makes known [the object] in its various specific modes.
Alternatively, *nirutti* is a word that is determined or fixed through the elucidation of its respective meaning.
The word *adhi* means "above. *Adhivacana* is a term for that which is above; above what?

Above the meaning that is to be made manifest—this meaning is evident. Alternatively, *adhivacana* is a term for that which is dependent (*adhīna*). On what is it dependent? It is dependent on the meaning. It is a "designation" (*paññatti*) in the sense of making the meaning known.
In this way, the application of terms such as *nirutti* (etymology) and so forth should be understood across all words. Otherwise, [the statement] "it touches... [would not hold].
The term *nirutti* (etymological derivation) applies only to words of selection such as "contact" (*phassa*) and so forth;
the term *adhivacana* (designation) applies only to expressions for specific individuals, such as Sirivaḍḍhaka and Dhanavaḍḍhaka;

and the term *paññatti* (conceptual description) would apply to words that indicate the same single meaning through various modes, such as "reasoning" (*takka*) and "applied thought" (*vitakka*). "Unmixed" (*asaṅkiṇṇā*) means not mixed.
Therefore he said: "not abandoned... not discarded. "Not being mixed" means they are not mixed, will not be mixed, and have not been mixed;

this is the meaning. "Unreviled" means not rejected. Since that which has transcended dissolution has necessarily transcended arising and so forth, it is therefore said: "precisely dissolution. Since [the dhamma] has also moved to another location...
It is called "transcended"; therefore, in order to show the absence of that [transcending], it is said: "without having moved to another place.
For wherever conditioned phenomena arise, right there they break up, cease, undergo change, and meet their destruction.
Hence he said: "changed... [and so on] ...perished. It has become unmanifest precisely because it has not been born.
They are called Vassabhajñas because they belong to the Vasabha clan. "Root-viewholders" (*mūla-diṭṭhigatikā*) means those who are the root-viewholders;

they are the first in this eon to give rise to such a view. "For one who reflects again and again" means for one who, having memorized and mastered the text associated with the doctrine of non-causality (*ahetuvāda*), investigates its meaning:
"There is no cause, there is no condition for the existence of beings..."
Wrong mindfulness settles upon the object of a dogmatic view that proceeds in such a manner as "for the sake of defilement" and so forth;
and regarding the meaning acquired through hearsay— such as "there are no causes"— which presents itself to the mind in its own form through reflections on those aspects,
as if with a physical grasp, one arrives at the state of being satisfied by reflection, thinking "it is just so," due to long-standing habituation.

When one repeatedly and habitually indulges in that which has been grasped by the Tathāgata through contemplation and acceptance, there arises—associated with the acquisition of that [wrong] view—a craving accompanied by wrong mindfulness.
This craving, which is undertaken by wrong thought, propped up by wrong effort, and which perceives what is not of such a nature as being "of such a nature," comes to rest.
It does so by obtaining its respective conditions, such as thought and the rest.
By way of being resolved upon that object, having abandoned lack of one-pointedness, the mind becomes as if fixed in one-pointedness through wrong concentration (*micchāsamādhi*).

For it should be understood that even this [wrong concentration], when its power of development has been acquired through specific conditions, performs a function similar to that of true concentration in such instances, just as in the case of piercing hair and so forth.
Indeed, many times in previous stages, by means of that mode [of practice]...
When the javana-moments are occurring, seven javanas run in the very last javana-moment. Therein, in the first [moment] he is curable;
likewise in the second and so forth. But when the seventh javana is reached, he becomes incurable. Therefore he said, "while relishing," and so on.
"In these two places" means in both of these instances.

Regarding the phrase "or the present": here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning. By this, it includes such passages as, "That which is called 'the future,' this is not the future," and so forth.
"Those too" means that even those Vassa and Bhañña did not conceive [of them as such], because they could not transcend worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*).
Therefore he said, "But the past... and so on. It is a designation (*paṇṇatti*) established in relation to the aggregates (*khandhā*).
The commentary on the *Niruttipathasutta* is finished.
The commentary on the *Upāyavagga* is finished.
7. The *Arahantavagga*.
1. Commentary on the *Upādiyamāna Sutta* 63.
"Grasping" means grasping by way of thinking, "This is mine," and so forth. "With a snare" means with the snare of lust (*rāga-pāsa*).
For Māra considers that very thing to be his "Māra-snare. Thus he said: "The snare that moves through the air, which roams the mind. One who does not grasp is called "liberated."
Because of the total absence of any aggregate (khandha).
The commentary on the *Upādiyamāna-sutta* is finished.
2–6. Commentary on the *Maññamāna-sutta* and others.
64–68. By the passage beginning with “This is mine,” [the text refers to] conceiving (*maññanā*) and delighting (*abhinandanā*). “Craving and desire” (*taṇhā-chando*) means craving itself is desire;
for that craving is called *taṇhā* in the sense of craving (*taṇhāyana*), and it is called *chando* in the sense of being desirous (*chandikata*).

The fourth [section] is stated by way of the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*), the fifth by way of the characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*), and the sixth by way of the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*). The remainder applies to all three as well.
"Exactly the same" means "the method is the same," as it was stated.
The commentary on the Maññamāna Sutta and others is finished.
7. Commentary on the Anattaniya Sutta.
69. "Anattaniyan" means not belonging to a self. Therefore he said, "not one's own property.
The commentary on the *Anattaniya Sutta* is finished.
8–10. Commentary on the *Rajanīyasaṇṭhita Sutta*, etc.
70–72. *Rajanīyena* means by that which is highly alluring, which gives rise to lust. Therefore he said, "by way of being a condition for lust.
These [discourses] were delivered in the *Rāhula-saṃyutta* by way of the questions of the Elder Rāhula;

here they are presented by way of the questions of the Elders Rādha and Surādha, though the text is identical in all respects. Therefore he said, "they are to be understood in the same manner as already stated."
The commentary on the Suttas beginning with "Rajanīyasaṇṭhita" is finished.
The commentary on the Arahantavagga is finished.
8. Khajjanīyavagga.
1–3. Commentary on the *Assāda-sutta* and others (73–75).
Only the Four Noble Truths are taught here, because the teaching proceeds by way of both the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth, as well as the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth.
For gratification is the truth of the origin, the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) is the truth of suffering, and the escape (*nissaraṇa*) consists of both the truth of the path and the truth of cessation.

This same meaning has already been stated: in the second sutta, the gratification (*assāda*) is the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*), the danger (*ādīnava*) is the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*), the subsiding (*atthaṅgama*) is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*), and the escape (*nissaraṇa*) is the truth of the path (*maggasacca*)—this is the meaning already stated. The third [sutta] is stated specifically with reference to the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).
The commentary on the *Assādasutta* and the others is finished.
4. Commentary on the Arahantasutta 76.
"As many abodes of beings as there are": in each respective class of beings, those very beings are called "abodes of beings" in the sense of being their dwelling place.
By this he shows that among all those abodes of beings, these are the foremost, these are the best—namely, these who are Arahants.
“By the same method as before” means by the method stated in the previous *Sattatthānakosalla-sutta*.
“By the elucidations of its meaning” refers both to the elucidations of the meaning of that aforementioned sutta—such as “Having fully understood the five aggregates, craving for them does not exist;
the conceit ‘I am’ is utterly cut off”—and to [the verse] beginning with “Unshaken are you...”
And by such passages as "their minds are undisturbed," which illustrate the specific excellence [of their state].
Because they possess an exceptional happiness included within jhāna, the path, and the fruit, they are called "happy"; thus he says, "jhāna... happy.

Regarding the phrase "craving does not exist for them," it is stated that craving which produces suffering in the states of misery (apāya) does not exist for them. [This refers to] the root of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Because of the absence of craving, it is said here: “Delight is not found in them.

Regarding the phrase “of this too,” by means of the word *pi* (“too”), the absence of craving rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) should be understood as being included along with the absence of suffering;

for it is precisely because of that [absence] that they are said to be “absolutely happy” through the attainment of Nibbāna without residue. This occurs through the mode of proceeding such as “I am superior,” and so forth.
It is ninefold. "By knowledge" means by the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga-ñāṇa*).
"Having attained arahantship. "Unstained" means unsmeared. "Become Brahmas" means having reached the state of a Brahma;
or, "become from the Brahma," that is, from the noble path-knowledge, they are born into the noble birth. The seven true qualities (*saddhamma*) are their range, their sphere of activity.
These are those whose range is the seven true Dhammas.
They are said to have "a course free from fear" because there is no fear for them from any quarter.

[They are endowed] with the ten factors beginning with right view and ending with right liberation and right knowledge. And they are characterized by the four reasons beginning with "he commits no offense."
“Craving does not exist for them”—this too is a demonstration of the great benefit of the abandonment of craving. Therefore he said:
“Even the craving that acts as a slave does not exist for them.
They do not waver with such thoughts as “I am superior,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "above, across, and below": the first method proceeds by taking the personal existence (*attabhāva*) as its object through the medium of form, beginning with the words "above is said," and so forth.
The second method proceeds by taking the manifestation of phenomena (*dhamma-pavatti*) as its object according to the three periods of time.
The third method proceeds by taking the entire world-system (*lokadhātu*) as its object according to location. "Buddhas" refers to those who have awakened to the four noble truths.
“Sīhanādasamodhānaṃ” means the compendium of lion’s roars. They are “anuttara” (unsurpassed) because there is no one in the world superior to oneself.
They are “asadi-sa” (without equal) in the sense that, let alone a man superior to oneself, even one who is equal does not exist.

Having transcended the entire round of existence and standing upon the summit of existence, they roar the lion’s roar in twenty-one ways by way of being happy through the bliss of liberation, and so forth.
The commentary on the Arahantasutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Arahantasutta. 77.
“Precisely the pure one” means having composed it as a pure and concise composition.
The commentary on the Second Arahat Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Siha Sutta: 78.
"Siha" refers to the lord of beasts who has received the name "Lion" because he endures dangers and slays his adversaries.
"Four" refers to four lions, who, despite being equal in their lion-like nature, are distinguished by differences such as their specific coloration.
Having now shown them by name, color, and food, the passage beginning with "grass-lion" is commenced in order to clarify the specific lion intended here through various classifications.
A lion whose food is grass is a "grass-lion" (*tiṇasīha*), formed by the elision of the latter member of the compound in the first term, just as [in other examples].
“*Sākapatthivo*”: because of its black color, it is like a black lion; likewise for the pale lion. Therefore he said:

“The black lion is like a black *gāvi* [serpent], and the pale lion is like a *gāvi* with the color of a withered leaf. It is called *kesarī* because it possesses a mane (*kesara*)—a mass of manes—like that of a red woolen blanket.
The construction is: “[with] feet and extremities as if treated with lac-dye.”

"By virtue of his majesty and great power, established through the influence of his past karma, he is the king of all herds of wild animals"—this was said with reference to the fact that "the lion’s dwelling and activity are thus.
"Having set it down level" means having placed it on the ground so that it is even on all sides.

"Having dragged it forward" means having pulled it toward the front. "Having brought it forward" means having carried it toward the face. "Destruction" (saṅkhāta) means ruin. A space of twenty *aṭṭhis* is an *usabha*.
“Equal lion” means a lion that is equal in birth and equal in portion. “I am equal” is merely a conventional expression; he does not fear even because of his equal radiance.

“Due to the strength of the view of self-identity” means due to the power of the view of self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which is the cause of egoism and serves as the sign for the overweening pride of strength, thinking: “Who else is superior to us? We alone are truly mighty.”
"Because of the abandoning of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*)" means that because the view of a personal body has been abandoned,
and because of the absence of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*),

and because attachment to self (*attasineha*) has been thoroughly eradicated, he does not fear. Having stated, "In such and such a way," meaning he described himself in various manners such as being like a lion, etc., the passage beginning with "He is a lion, indeed" was spoken in order to explain and demonstrate that meaning.

Since the state of Buddhahood was certain for the Lord of the World who had already made his resolution, having reached the stage of being destined for enlightenment, his previous states prior to the final awakening—
such as "the time of dwelling in the three palaces," "the time of giving his promise to King Magadha," and "the time of consuming the milk-rice"—
are shown to be like those of a lion. For even a designation of what has already occurred (*bhūta-upacāra*) may be applied to what is yet to be (*bhāvin*).

This is worldly usage. By taking both true knowledge (*bhūta-vijjā*) and other types of knowledge together on the basis of their commonality as "states of knowledge" (*vijjābhāva-sāmañña*), and treating them as already established prior to the contemplation of dependent origination—just as one treats a result that has already been produced—he says, "having purified the three knowledges.
It is said, "by churning with the knowledge of pairs," by way of the knowledge proceeding in both forward and reverse order.
"While dwelling there" means while dwelling at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.

"On the eleventh day" means on the eleventh day after the seven-week period had passed. "In the immovable cross-legged posture" refers to the seat upon which he sat in Isipatana for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
For that too is called the "adamantine seat" (*vajirāsana*) because it was the sitting posture for the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, which cannot be overturned by anyone.

It is called the immovable throne (acalapallaṅka). And in this context—namely, in this portion of the True Dhamma (saddhamma) set forth in the manner beginning with, "Bhikkhus, these two extremes..."—the sound of the Dhamma...
[pe] ...covered the ten-thousandfold world system by means of the resolve: "Let those standing everywhere hear it!
By way of sixteen aspects: "the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin..."
"the realization of cessation, and the development of the path"—thus, having set forth four aspects for each of the paths, [it is explained] by way of sixteen modes.
This has already been stated and need not be repeated here; therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained in that context.
Furthermore, since the Blessed One is called "Tathāgata" for eight other reasons as well, [this is mentioned] in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā and other such works.
The meaning of the term *tathāgata-pada* has already been stated; therefore, its meaning should be understood according to the method explained therein.

Although the Blessed One did not become fully enlightened merely by sitting on the seat of awakening (*bodhipallaṅka*), nevertheless, it was while sitting in that very posture that he dispelled all dangers and became fully enlightened.
For this reason, it is called the "unconquered seat" (*aparājita-pallaṅka*).
It is so called. Therefore, having said "as far as the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka)," not being satisfied with that, he said "as far as the knowledge of the path of arahantship.

Thus, regarding the word *iti* in the phrase "iti rūpaṃ," the term *iti* has the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). By means of it, matter is shown according to its own nature (*sarūpato*), its measure (*parimāṇato*), and its delimitation (*paricchedato*);

thus he said, "This is matter," and so forth. For by the words "this is matter," matter—distinguished as the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*)—is shown according to its own nature.
It has been shown. By the phrase "so much form," it is shown by way of its measure. And by demonstrating the absolute nature of that measure, it is said: "There is no form beyond this.
"By way of individual essence" means by way of its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*). "By way of own-nature" means by way of its own function (*sakicca*).
"By way of limit" means by way of the limit of its measure. "By way of delimitation" means [the extent] of the space in which its occurrence takes place.
"By way of delimitation" means by way of reaching the conclusion. All of that has been shown according to the aforementioned classification.
"This is the origin of matter" means this—namely, nutriment and so forth—is the origin of matter.
Therefore he said, "To this extent," and so on. "Cessation" means destruction. And [the statement] "From the arising of nutriment... from the cessation of nutriment" is indeed specific (non-common).
Having taken [the first], he includes the remainder by means of the word "etc.
(*ādi*). "Adorned with the fifty characteristics" means embellished with the fifty characteristics of arising and passing away, because of the inclusion of both origination and cessation.
"Because of the destruction of the taints" (*khīṇāsavattā*) is due to the complete and partial exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*); for even non-returners (*anāgāmin*) possess fear.
"And there is no fear in the mind": this refers to the knowledge of spiritual urgency (*ñāṇasaṃvega*), which is the knowledge of the manifestation of fear.
"But of the other gods," however, he says with reference to those gods who have not yet exhausted their taints (*akhīṇāsava*). "Sir" (*bho*) is merely a form of address regarding the Dhamma;

it is merely such verbal address. "Wheel" (*cakra*) is the wheel of the Teacher’s command; because that has come forth from the Dhamma, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). Therein, for the noble disciples...
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it has come from the Dhamma of penetration; for others, it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it has come from the Dhamma of teaching.
Since knowledge is primary in both types, it is stated from the standpoint of knowledge: "both penetrative knowledge and teaching knowledge.
Now, in order to show those two kinds of knowledge according to their specific nature, it is said: "Penetrative knowledge is... and so forth. And because of this...
Because his knowledge was thoroughly penetrated, the Blessed One was capable of showing those sixty thousand methods to those who were to be trained;
therefore, considering that those sixty thousand methods were established together with that very knowledge, he said, "He penetrated by means of sixty thousand methods.
"Three turns" refers to: "This is suffering," and "It is to be fully understood."
And "it has been fully understood"—thus it has three turnings and twelve aspects.
The Blessed One brings forth that very knowledge of the teaching. "Peerless" means devoid of any person who could serve as a counterpart. "Of one and the same kind" means without variation.
The commentary on the Sīha Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Khajjanīya-sutta* 79.

"By way of insight" (*vipassanāvasena*): Having recollected the present aggregates of form, feeling, and so forth, the thought, "In the past, too, I was possessed of such feeling," constitutes insight (*vipassanā*) because it demonstrates the lack of distinction between past form, feeling, and so forth, and those of the present. Of that insight...
By way of this: showing the reason for the negation made in the words, "This is not by way of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)," he said, "But by way of direct knowledge," and so forth.

Those things called "bound up with the aggregates" (*khandhapaṭibaddhā*) are such as lineage, complexion, beauty, and so on. "Recalling in this way" means recalling by way of the aforementioned insight (*vipassanā*).
This is because it was stated that the recollection pertains only to phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*).
The section titled “The Chapter on Emptiness” (*suññatāpabba*) has been stated.

Since those very things—form and so forth—are neither self nor belonging to a self, being essenceless and powerless, they are therefore empty of them; the state of being that is emptiness (*suññatā*). To show its characteristic, such as being subject to change (*ruppana*), etc., [the author] says:
“Kiñca? (And what?). This is the nominative case used in the sense of a reason that indicates a cause; thus he says: “‘Kiñca? is a question regarding the cause; by what...”
“By what reason should one speak of ‘form’? Here, “this” refers to this class of phenomena consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives.
“By what reason is it called ‘form’? means: depending on what reason is it designated as “form”? “Enumeration of reasons” means the pointing out of the reason.
It is called “form” (*rūpa*) because it is “affected” (*ruppati*); here, being affected means the production of a change through the encounter with opposing conditions such as cold and so forth.
Therefore he said, "Even by cold," and so forth. "At the foot of the mountain" means at the foot of the Cakkavāḷa mountain;
it stands there like a wall rising high above. For indeed, beings remain there hanging down.

"Come within the reach of the hand" means come near, having approached within the range of the hand. "Therein" means among those beings who have come within the reach of the hand. "Having been cut off" means having been released from the attainment of unconsciousness (mucchā).

Or [it means] having cut it off by way of severing the limbs and members. Regarding the phrase "in extremely salty water," the state of being "extremely salty" may have been stated with reference specifically to its extreme coldness due to the absence of the heat of the sun;
for that water which lasts for an eon (*kappa*), rained down by great clouds that bring about prosperity and sustains the earth, cannot become salty like the water that destroys the eon.
"If that were so, it would be fitting for even the earth to melt away. Mahisakaraṭṭha is a certain kingdom in a region of the Himālayas.
"In the Great Niraya of Avīci" refers to the Avīci hell when it is in its state of full intensity. "On the back of the Gaṅgā" means on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
"Moving along" explains the meaning of the word *sarīsapa* (reptile). "This" refers to the state of being afflicted (*ruppana*). "Just as hardness... [refers to the nature of solidity].

The specific characteristic (*paccatta-lakkhaṇa*) of earth is its deformation; such deformation is the specific characteristic of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-khandha*), meaning its characteristic of being a state of intrinsic nature.

"Similar to the former" means similar to what was stated regarding the previous aggregate of form. That [characteristic] is to be understood by the same method as stated in the passage beginning with, "What is the inquiry into the cause?
Pleasure is a desirable object. [This refers to] the feelings (*vedanā*) of pleasure and so forth. By way of condition...
By way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*). This is the meaning: "That which has a pleasant object is called 'pleasant'"; this is the meaning.

For this is an expression by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound. "Experiences" (*vedayatī*) means "feels" (*anubhavati*). "Having the characteristic of being experienced" (*vedayitalakkhaṇā*) means having the characteristic of feeling (*anubhavanalakkhaṇā*).
"A blue flower" (*nīlapuppha*) means a flower of blue color. "Or on cloth" (*vatthe vā*) means on blue cloth. By the word "or" (*vā*), it includes the element of color (*vaṇṇadhātu*) and so forth.
Causing either absorption (appanā) or access concentration (jhāna) to arise. "Perception that arises" refers to any perception arising in relation to a blue visible object-base;
it is what is called "dispersed perception. "For the sake of form-ness" means for the state of being form.
"Only the basis that has the nature of gruel" means only that physical base which possesses the nature of gruel. "For the state of gruel" means for the condition of being gruel.

"A person cooks" means: just as a person cooks or prepares a substance such as rice-gruel for the purpose of rice-gruel and so forth, so too, within this collection of phenomena whose intrinsic nature is to be afflicted (ruppanādi), that collection of phenomena dominated by volition (cetanā) acts as a specific condition for their continued occurrence;
it thus conditions, deposits, and brings about those [phenomena] when they are being fully formed by their respective conditions.
Therefore he said, “By conditions,” and so forth. “Matter itself” means the very nature of matter, not any other nature.
“It conditions” means it makes those other conditioned phenomena its own condition in an eminent and thorough way. “Approaches,” “sustains,” and “exerts effort” are synonyms for that same process;
for conditioning itself is what is meant by exertion and the rest. “Produces” refers to those phenomena.

The meaning is that it serves as a condition for production by way of being subject to deformation (*ruppana*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) characterized by intending":

this is stated because the phenomena of the aggregate of volitional formations have volition as their principal factor. For indeed, when the Blessed One was analyzing the aggregate of volitional formations in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, he analyzed it as volition alone.
*Vātiṅgaṇa* is the *brahatiphala*. *Caturassavallī* is the *tivutālatā*. *Akhārika* means that which is devoid of a salty taste; this refers to leaves, fruits, and so forth.
That in which a salty taste predominates is called "salty," as in the expression "salty gruel" (*loṇayāgu*), and so on. [This refers to] tastes distinguished as sour and the like.
"By way of grasping the aspect and the shape" means by way of grasping aspects such as blue, yellow, and so forth, and by way of grasping shapes such as round, square, and so forth.
"Even without aspect and shape" means without the aspect and shape; that is, even setting those aside.

"By way of grasping the individual distinction" means by way of grasping the specific differentiation of each respective object. "From non-delusion" means according to reality (*yāthāvato*). It is called a "distinction" because it illuminates a distinguished meaning.
This state (dhamma) is undifferentiated because it demonstrates non-differentiation. Therefore he said, "The distinction is to be understood. For knowing (*jānana*) is undifferentiated;
it is the prefixes that differentiate it from the compound term. Thus, the term "perceiving" (*sañjānana*) indicates the mere grasping of an aspect as the sign for recognition (*paccabhijñāṇa*);
the term "discerning" (*vijānana*) indicates the grasping of an object more distinguished than that; and the term "understanding" (*pajānana*)—
But it also makes one understand an awakening that is even more distinguished than that in its mode. Therefore he said, "Of that too," and so forth.
"Mere perception of the object" means merely the observation of an object distinguished as blue and so on. By the restrictive particle (*eva*), he excludes the penetration of characteristics.
Therefore he said, "Impermanent," and so forth. For one who is practicing insight with consciousness associated with knowledge, [this is] through insight.
Since insight occurs even with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge when there is proficiency [in concentration], he said:

"And it brings about the penetration of the characteristics by way of impermanence and so forth. By "penetration" (*paṭivedha*), he means merely the acquisition (*upaladdhi*) of the characteristic, not the act of piercing through (*paṭivijjhana*).
Therefore, he said: "But having ascended," and so forth. "Having ascended" means having caused [the mind] to ascend; it also brings about the manifestation of the path.

Because its intrinsic nature is non-delusion. Just as at the time of penetrating the characteristics [of phenomena], it proceeds by way of the characteristic of perceiving and by way of what is appropriate to that perception, so too this [consciousness] should be understood to proceed by way of the characteristic of cognizing and by way of what is appropriate to that.
Now, in order to clarify this matter through the similes of the money-changer and others, he says "Just as... and so forth. "Gold" (hirañña) is said...
A *kahāpaṇa* is a coin. One appointed to the knowledge of gold is a *heraññika* (money-changer).

One whose intelligence (*buddhi*) regarding worldly convention (*vohāra*) has not arisen or developed is one of "unborn intelligence" (*ajātabuddhi*), namely, a young child. A village-dwelling man skilled in worldly convention is a *gāmikapurisa* (village-man).

It is called "enjoyment and use" (*upabhogaparibhoga*) because it is fit for enjoyment and use. It is "false" (*kūṭa*) because it is made of copper or bronze. It is "clever" (*cheṅka*) because of its great value. It is "worthless" (*karaṭa*) because of its meager value.

It is subtle because its essence is low. And here, just as a money-changer knows a coin in its various aspects—such as its being genuine or counterfeit, its material quality, and even its place of origin by means of seeing its form and so forth—and thus knows it in many ways;
so too, wisdom knows and penetrates the object in its manifold modes. Along with that wisdom, the consciousness occurring together with it also knows the object as its respective domain.

Thus, this distinction in their knowledge—which is not within the domain of others but is the domain of the Buddhas alone—is clarified by the *Milindapañha* with the words beginning "Therefore he said," which is easy to understand.
Because it was stated that phenomena (dhammas) which are empty of self are merely phenomena (dhammamattatā), it is said, "having taught the characteristic of non-self.
And if the lower paths have been attained, yet because arahantship has not been attained, it is said, "by way of a mere portion."
That which was stated was begun in this section to show the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*), while the other two characteristics are intended as its corollaries.
For, in this context, through the teaching beginning with "What do you think, monks? and so forth, among the three characteristics, this very one—
It cannot be said that this is shown as being secondary while that is primary; therefore it was said, "in order to show them by combining the three characteristics.
"He diminishes" means he turns away from states leading to accumulation, because he fulfills the practice leading exclusively to diminution.
Hence he said, "he does not accumulate," and so forth. "He destroys the round" means he disperses it.
"He leads to non-perception" means he causes it not to appear. "He does not accumulate" means he does not increase it. "That very same" refers to that very cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

"He relinquishes" means he discards it. "He scatters" means he destroys it. "He fans away" means he makes the mass of fire known as the three cycles of existence free from smoke and free from heat; thus he says, "he extinguishes."
"Seeing thus," and so forth, was said with the intention of teaching the noble disciple established in the fruit of non-returning how to attain the fruit of the supreme path;
[the Blessed One] said, "I shall show one who has destroyed the round and stands as one whose taints are utterly exhausted.
This very demonstration of the future state of one whose taints are exhausted, and all this preceding teaching, is a discourse on pure insight (suddhavipassanā), together with the first path.
Showing that this is a discourse on insight (vipassanā) concerning phenomena that are like lightning, he said, “By this much [of a] point,” and so forth.
They pay homage indeed with great reverence and high esteem; therefore he said, “Homage to you, O noble steed among men,” and so on.
Therein, showing an illustration, he said, “Just as toward the Venerable Elder Nīta,” and in order to clarify that meaning, he said, “The elder,” and so forth.

In that context, "even on the tip of the razor" means that while applying himself to meditation by way of the fivefold skin-work (tacapañcaka) as soon as the razor’s edge is placed upon the head for the purpose of shaving the hair, he attains Arahantship.
"Brahma-palaces" (brahmavimānāni) refers to the celestial mansions that serve as the dwellings of the Brahmas.
The commentary on the *Khajjanīya Sutta* is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Piṇḍolya Sutta 80.
It is called an *apakaraṇa* because one is removed (*apakarīyati*) by means of it; thus, it is a "footstep" (*pada*). In meaning, *apakaraṇa*, *pakaraṇa*, and *kāraṇa* are one and the same.
Therefore he said, "for some reason or other. "Having led out" means having removed [the person] from being in one's own immediate vicinity.
"Acting accordingly" means: "In this way, having refrained from doing even such an unseemly thing as this, they will practice rightly in the future.
"Having gained strength" means having gained the power of knowledge (*ñāṇabala*).
"Single or double efforts" (*ekadvīhikā*): the effort, approach, or movement of one by one and of two by two is "single or double effort."
Therefore he said: “Each one alone and two by two. It was stated that “they might even play” because such activity could also occur when ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) are gathered together.
By way of supposition, it is said that even well-behaved monks act in this manner directed toward the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Between the Yugandhara mountain and the others is the ocean called Sīdantara. It is said that there the wind does not blow;
whatever falls into the Sīdantara river merely dissolves and sinks away. Therefore, the Yugandhara and other mountains standing surrounding it are also called Sīda-mountains.
With reference to this, it was said: "The great ocean situated within the Sīdantara."
“Because of food” means because of material gain (*āmiṣa*), for the sake of things such as ghee and oil;
it refers to their distribution. “Last” means inferior. Therefore he said “vile,” for what is intended here is that which is vile:
“The jackal among beasts, and the crow among birds;”
As in the passages beginning with: “The castor-oil plant is the lowest among trees; three ends have come together.
It means he practices sorcery (*ulati* = *abhicarati*). That by which one curses is a curse (*abhisāpa*). The basis for the curse is mendicancy (*piṇḍolya*).

That which has purpose (*attha*) and power (*vasa*) as its essence is "purposeful" (*atthavasa*), meaning the cause; that [cause] also exists in those [cases], and they are engaged therein, thus they are "those concerned with the purpose" (*atthavasikā*).
They have entered within the interior of the heart by way of the bases of sorrow.
"Covetous" means one whose nature is to covet. "One of abundant lust" refers to one who possesses lust both through constant occurrence and through its intensity.
"By way of putrefaction" means by way of being rotten; for when ill-will arises, it makes the mind foul-smelling, not...
"Of a pleasant and agreeable nature. "Like a crow that has dropped its food":

this is said because the crow's loss of mindfulness is manifested by the lack of protection for the place where the food was set down, not because of the act of dropping the food itself. "Unsteady" means one whose mind is unsteady.
"The task to be done with wood" means the duty to be performed by means of wood.
This is for the purpose of showing that because they are produced by evil thoughts, they must be abandoned without remainder.

With the intention that since two [types] have been mentioned, it is appropriate to say that one is "prior" (pubbabhāga) and the other is "mixed" (missaka), the passage beginning with "And here" was stated.
The ancients maintain that these should be understood as being mixed one by one, in the sense that they cease for one who develops them in this way.
In the teaching above, consisting of three repetitions, only signless concentration (animitta-samādhi) is illustrated. Therefore he said, "To such an extent.
"Free from blemish" means free from passion and so forth.
The commentary on the Piṇḍolya Sutta is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Pālileyya Sutta 81.
*Pariyādiṇṇarūpacittā*: whose minds have been seized, exhausted, and captivated by lust and other defilements.

The Blessed One’s movements were known through familiarity. The Teacher partook [of the food] out of compassion, thinking, "In this way, he will be liberated from an evil rebirth. *Aññatra*: except for; without.
"By the elephant" means by the Buddha-elephant, who is equipped with a goad; for that very reason, by means of a mind that has become straight.

In this way, the mind of an elephant—one whose tusks are like a ploughshare—is calmed. Regarding this, he states the reason: "When one delights in the forest. By this, he speaks of a commonality of delight through physical seclusion (*kāyaviveka*).
"By its own nature" means by its very character, spontaneously.
"The destruction of the taints" here refers to Arahantship; and since that occurs immediately after the supreme path, he said, "the fruit of Arahantship immediately following the path.
"Investigation" is intended here as the wisdom of teaching, and since that operates in many ways, it was stated [as follows].
“By way of investigation” (*vicayaso*): although it occurs many times, because it is simply investigation (*vicaya*), the meaning is stated as “by means of investigation.

The “Dhamma of the Dispensation” (*sāsanadhammo*) is the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhammo*) that elucidates the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth. The reflection (*parivitakko*) arose:
“Regarding which knowledge [is there] concerning the Dhamma taught by me, having thus defined it by its divisions, such as ‘the four foundations of mindfulness’ and so on?”
The intention is that for some, doubt still persists regarding the thought, "There is an ending of the taints in the interval.
"View itself is the contemplation" means "view-contemplation" (*diṭṭhisamanupassanā*). "Volitional formation of view" (*diṭṭhisaṅkhāra*) means a volitional formation conditioned by view.
For that very reason, it is said, "That volitional formation is born from that," meaning that volitional formation is born from that craving. Thus, among these four...
The formation of views is a formation that arises with views as its decisive support. "Contact accompanied by ignorance" means contact associated with ignorance.
Thus, in this context, the Blessed One shows the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness as belonging exclusively to the side of formations.
"In these instances" refers to the passage beginning with "Here, monks, an uninstructed worldling... and continuing up to "...there will be no more for me."

“In this much extent. “The views already grasped”: this refers to the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), such as the eternalist view that occurs in the form “That is the self, that is the world,” etc., as well as the annihilationist view that occurs in the form “I shall not be, and it shall not be for me,” etc.—that is, the views grasped in various ways.
By means of the teaching beginning with “Thus, monks, even that conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) is impermanent,” he causes [the listener] to relinquish them.
"He has arrived. Because he analyzes the views that have arisen right there, it should be understood that this teaching proceeds according to the inclination of the individual.
Its pedagogical excellence lies in leading [the listener] to Arahantship through twenty-three stages.
"The formation born from that" refers to the formation associated with doubt, which is born from craving that serves as the condition for that doubt.

If it were said that a formation is "born from that" (tatojo) because it is produced from that craving by way of such conditions as co-nascence, this would be shown to be improper; thus [the author] challenges this with:

"associated with craving... is born. The other [respondent], showing that here the aspect of decisive support (upanissaya) is intended, says "because it has not been abandoned," and explains that meaning with the words "for one who... and so forth. For [it is not] by craving...
Doubt arises. If there is no co-nascent condition (*sahajātaka*), then doubt must indeed arise from craving by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya*).
"Of views as well" means of the sixty-two types of views. Therefore he said, "In the four," and so forth.
By adding the twenty views of a personal identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), along with eternalism, annihilationism, and doubt, each [is considered] by way of impermanence.
Having shown insight and brought [the listener] to the state of Arahatship, the teaching was concluded; thus he said, "In twenty-three places," and so forth.
The commentary on the Pālileyya Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Puṇṇama Sutta.
82. It is called a *desa* (locus) because it is pointed out (*dissati*) and indicated (*apadissati*); it is the cause, and that should be understood as an indicative one.

For, although he wishes to know the intrinsic nature consisting of changeability (*ruppanādi*) and so forth, he first asks about its essential form (*sarūpa*), and then the specific distinction (*visesa*) of that must be asked;
thus, he first poses the question with "Are these... and so on. And here too, for that bhikkhu, it is precisely that specific distinction [which is being sought].
He shows that it is "the end. The intention is that he asks as if not knowing "their cause.
Because they originate from craving and desire as their root, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are mentioned;

here, specifically, craving-clinging (*taṇhupādāna*) is what is grasped, while the other [types of clinging] are included by that very mention because they are inseparable from it; thus, only desire and lust (*chandarāga*) are singled out.

This is the rejection of that objection. Even though the aggregates may not be co-nascent with the clingings and may not be the objects of clinging, he shows that clinging is indeed co-nascent with them and has them as its object;
for there is no clinging that is both non-co-nascent and non-objective. Now, in order to explain this matter further:
The passage beginning with “associated with craving” (taṇhāsampayuttasmiṃ) and so forth is indeed easy to understand. “By way of object” (ārammaṭo) means by way of making it an object.

Because there is an absence of the occurrence of desire and lust (chandarāga) in the form “May I have such a feeling” (evaṃvedano siyaṃ) for one who has [already] had the occurrence of desire and lust in the form “May I be such a person” (evaṃrūpo siyaṃ), the formations (saṅkhārā) are broken right there and then; therefore, [this applies] to the desire, lust, and so forth that have visible form and feeling as their objects.

Even though there is indeed a distinction between desire (*chanda*) and lust (*rāga*), because the question was not asked in connection with desire and lust—specifically in terms of their abandonment and so forth—it was said that "the connection does not fit.
Although it does not fit because the question concerned something else entirely, nevertheless, the question is indeed connected; for that very reason, the answer is also connected. In this regard:

He states the reason with the words “of this and that,” etc. By this, he shows that the questions and answers possess a continuous sequence (anusandhi) by way of the underlying intention and the connection [between them].
The commentary on the Puṇṇama Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Khajjanīya Vagga is finished.
9. Theravagga 1.
Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā 83.
*Paṭicca* means having made a dependence. “I am this” is the grasping of a view; “I am better” is the grasping of conceit.
And since these [states] exist by way of craving alone, craving too is both the condition for such a process and itself that very process;
thus it is said: "The triad of conceptual proliferation consisting of craving, conceit, and views proceeds in this manner as 'I am'.

Since the word *dahara* (young) can also refer to a small child, the term "youth" (*yuvā*) is stated to distinguish him from that. Furthermore, since even a youth might be one who lacks the habit of adornment, the term [is used] to distinguish him from that.
It is said, “one who is by nature fond of adornment. By this, he shows the existence of reflecting on the image of the face.
“Of him,” meaning of one looking into the surface of a mirror. “It would appear facing away”:
if he were standing facing the eastern direction, the image of the face would also appear facing the eastern direction; such is the meaning.
Even if another person were similar [to oneself], there would still be some dissimilarity;
thus it is said, "it would appear as being dissimilar in color and so forth. "A reflected image" (*nibhāsarūpa*) means a reflected form.
First, let such a reflected image appear in a bright disk made of bronze or other materials; but how is it in water? By what cause? Thus he asks.
He asks. The other, saying “due to the purity of the great elements,” shows that even there it is by means of the very luster obtained [from them].
And here, the worldling is like a man fond of adornment; the five aggregates are like the surface of a mirror and so forth;
the grasping “I am” is like the reflection of a face; and the visible form and so forth appearing based on the reflection of the face is like [the basis for] the grasping “I am.”

When there is [the conceit] "I am," there arise specific modes of grasping such as "I am superior" and so forth. *Abhisameta* means "fully understood"; or rather, this reading (*abhisamita*) itself is correct.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Tissa Sutta.
84. "Madhuraka" is said to mean "a heavy burden upon the body. Thus he said: "As if born with a madhuraka" means "as if a state of heaviness has arisen.
When there is heaviness, lightness has no place; likewise for malleability and wieldiness. Therefore it is said, "unwieldy.
The word "in the body" must be supplied [to complete the sense]. "They do not appear" means they do not manifest after having become visible. Hence he said: "not..."
“They become manifest. "Attending" means they stand near. "Is not seen" means it does not come within the range of perception.
"Great doubt" refers to uncertainty regarding the eight bases and the sixteen bases; it does not arise because the roots of merit have reached full maturity.

Having extracted the phrase "this is a designation for sensual pleasures," the passage beginning with "Just as... was spoken in order to clarify the intention with which the Blessed One brought forward the example of a swamp that is "sloping toward" as an illustration of sensual pleasures.
The commentary on the Tissa Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Yamaka Sutta 85.

A "view" (*diṭṭhi*) itself is a "course of view" (*diṭṭhigata*), just as one speaks of "feces-deposit" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-deposit" (*muttagata*). It is called a "course of view" because it is grasped as a being separate from the aggregates (*khandha*).

"Agitated" means agitated by the disease known as wrong view. "Having asserted" means that, being unable to state his own position with such certainty as he did in the presence of those monks—saying "Indeed, it is so"—he was unable to speak thus in the very presence of the Elder Sāriputta.
"The duty of inquiry" (anuyogavatta) is the disclosure, according to reality, of one's own conviction through contemplation and acceptance when one is engaged in an inquiry.
"Regarding the Elder’s inquiry, ‘the ground’ (bhūmi) refers to the locative designation for the question posed by the Elder, beginning with: ‘What do you think, friend Yamaka?
‘If that, friend’ (sace taṃ āvuso) refers to this statement, namely, ‘If that, friend,’ and so forth. ‘That’ (etaṃ) refers to the Elder Yamaka.
‘Another’ (aññaṃ) refers to Arahatship. Speaking in the manner of what ought to be said, it is in fact Arahatship."
He speaks with the intention that one is called "one who gives a prophecy" (byākaronto).
"Of this first path" means of this first path which you have just now attained at the conclusion of the teaching on the three turnings.
"By the four bonds" means by the four bonds of arising harm: as self, as dear, as neutral, and as enemy.
"Approaches" (*upeti*) means that one grasps by means of the approach of craving (*taṇhūpāya*) and the approach of views (*diṭṭhūpāya*); one reaches the objective basis for craving and views.

"Grasps" (*upādiyati*) means that one takes hold with a firm grip. "Adheres" (*adhitiṭṭhati*) means that one stands having become dogmatically attached (*abhinivissa*). How so? Thinking, "This is my self.
"These are my enemies" means that these five aggregates of clinging—form, feeling, and so forth—are my enemies because they bring about harm.
Having known by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "Having applied [the mind] to insight" means having applied the aggregates to insight.
The commentary on the Yamaka Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Anurādha Sutta.
86. "Of that very monastery" means: of that very monastery in the Great Forest where the Blessed One was dwelling.

"These" refers to the followers of other sects (*aññatitthiyā*). Because this Elder did not set aside the question that ought to be set aside by way of its being a matter for setting aside, therefore [the text says]:
"The followers of other sects... said this. For this reason, it says: "Knowing the tenets of the Dispensation in part."
It is already included therein because it has been established even before that; therefore he said, "Because it is its root. "Thus" means:
"I proclaim both suffering and the cessation of suffering"—thus. "The very cycle and the turning away from the cycle" means:
the cycle is explained by way of the contemplation of the five aggregates, while the turning away from the cycle is explained by such passages as "seeing thus," and so forth.
The commentary on the Anurādha Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Vakkali Sutta: 87.
“A great affliction arose in the middle of the city” means that as he was coming through the middle of the city, a great [affliction] originating from karma arose.
Affliction arises. "From all sides, his heart sank" means it trembled in every part.
"To maintain his posture" means to carry out the postures distinguished by lying down, sitting, and so forth. "They turn back" means they recede;
the meaning is that they decline. "They attain" means they increase. The body of qualities of the Teacher has its root in the attainment of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma.
Having stated this, it was said: “For the body is ninefold... [etc.]... so called. Just as the body of sentient beings is rooted in rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
“The monastery built on Black Rock” is *kāḷasilāvihāra*. “For the sake of the path and liberation” means for the attainment of the supreme path and liberation (*aggamaggavimokkha*).
“Devas” refers to the deities of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*). It is called “not deficient” because there is no occurrence of death among worldlings (*puthujjana*) there. Therefore he said:
“‘The Elder, it is said,’ and so forth. ‘One or two knowledges’: one or two reviewing knowledges (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) necessarily arise by their very nature;
this is the natural law (*dhammatā*). The reviewing of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna arises precisely upon emerging from each respective path.
The expression ‘one or two’ is stated for the purpose of showing that they have indeed arisen.”
The state of smoking is the appearance of smoke; likewise, the state of being dimmed by darkness.
The commentary on the Vakkali Sutta is finished.
6. Commentary on the Assaji Sutta.

88. *Passambhitvā* means having ceased. *No ca svāhaṃ* means "not indeed, I [am]. One falls away because of the nature of being subject to agitation (*kuppadhamma*). *Etaṃ* refers to that which has mere concentration as its essence;
however, regarding mere virtue (*sīlamatta*), there is simply nothing to be said. *Kathaṃ hoti* means how does delight (*abhinandanā*) arise?
Having encountered suffering, one longs for pleasure as the cause for the arising of suffering, thinking: "In this way, may my fever of suffering..."
"It will not be. "In whatever portion" means by whichever part. Having stated, "One indeed yearns for suffering," he states the reason for that:
"Because of the change of pleasure," and so forth. When pleasure undergoes transformation, there is the suffering of the change of pleasure;
therefore, one who delights in pleasure, in actual fact, delights in suffering.
The commentary on the Assaji Sutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Khemaka Sutta 89.
"Belonging to a self" means that which belongs to a self as imagined by those who hold wrong views. Therefore he said: "the collection of requisites belonging to oneself."
Craving and conceit have been overcome because of not yet attaining Arahantship; conceit based on views has not been overcome, nor have sensual lust and ill will.
It is said that the Elder Khemaka was a non-returner (anāgāmī), though some say he was a once-returner (sakadāgāmī). "By wandering" means by moving about.
Therefore he said, "by going and coming again and again. "By going and coming four times" means four times.
"By going and by coming. Therefore he said: "On that day he wandered for a distance of two yojanas.
"Having known" means having known the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). "The Elder" refers to the Elder Khemaka.
"He says 'I am form' alone" means he speaks having made the aggregate of form itself the basis for the grasping "I am. Craving and conceit have been overcome.

*Aṇusahagata* means having reached a subtle state. Therefore, he said "subtle" (*sukhuma*). The three contemplations (*anupassanā*) are like the three alkaline substances because they purify the defilement of the mind.

By "fragrances of virtue" such as the fragrance of morality (*sīla*), etc. "To speak" means to speak by way of enumeration (*uddesa*). "To reveal" means to reveal that meaning by way of detailed exposition (*niddesa*).
"To make known" means to make it known by way of the underlying cause (*kāraṇa*). "To establish" means to cause it to be spoken. "To make open" refers to providing an illustration (*udāharaṇa*).
"To explain" means to make it clear. "To analyze well" means to analyze thoroughly through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
"To make plain" means to make that meaning manifest through applications (*upanaya*) and conclusions (*nigama*).
"By another mental application" means by the mental application of one liberated through insight (*vipassanā-vimutta*).
The commentary on the Khemaka Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Channa Sutta 90.

*Makkhī* means one who possesses *makkha*, characterized by the concealing of virtues. *Paḷāsī* means one who possesses *paḷāsa*, characterized by contentiousness. *Etaṃ avoca* means he said this: “May they exhort me... [and so on]... may they see [me].”
“Thera” refers to the Elder Channa. One might even find fault with someone due to one’s own poor grasp [of the teaching].

Therefore it was said: “Thus, it seems, this thought occurred to them,” and so forth. “Making it entirely free from fault” means: having made it suitable from the very beginning, we shall speak of the True Dhamma.
“Agitation as clinging” means: agitation through fear is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). When there is no-self, that which is done by what is not-self...
The thought, "Kamma will touch me," gives rise to fear and agitation as well as clinging to views.
"He turns back" means he turns back from the insight (vipassanā) he had begun; the meaning is that he was unable [to proceed].
But why did this happen to him while he was devoted to insight? To explain the reason for this, he says, "It is said that... and so forth. "Thus."
“The thought ‘What indeed is my self? does not occur [to him]. “There was sufficient confidence” means there was the trust expressed by saying, “Teach me the Dhamma.
The construction is: “He saw this Kaccāyana Sutta. The passage beginning with “The world, Kaccāna, is dependent on a duality” is for the purpose of unraveling views.
The passage beginning with “Without approaching either of these two extremes, Kaccāna” is for the purpose of illustrating the power of the Buddha.
The commentary on the Channa-sutta is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Rāhula-sutta and others. 91–92.
Regarding these suttas: "Brought here" means they were brought into this chapter by the compilers of the collection.
The commentary on the Rāhulasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Theravagga is finished.
10. The Pupphavagga.

1. Commentary on the *Nadīsutta* (The River Discourse) 93. *Pabbateyyā*: "Coming from a mountain. For that very reason, it is "flowing down" (*ohārinī*). By this, its fierce current is shown. "It goes far" (*dūraṅgamā*); by this, its great flood is shown. "In the stream" (*sote*) means in the stream of saṃsāra.

"By four graspings" (*catūhi gāhehi*) means by the four graspings that proceed according to the method beginning with "one regards form as self. "By way of destruction" (*palujjanattā*) means by way of being cut off. "Attaining calamities such as sorrow" (*sokādibyasanappattī*) means the arising of misfortunes such as sorrow.
The commentary on the Nadīsutta is finished.
2. Commentary on the Pupphasutta 94.
*Vivadati* means he engages in dispute. *Vadanto* means speaking in a manner that does not accord with reality. He disputes according to the true nature of things (*dhammatā*).
He speaks having made a contradiction. "Worldly phenomena" (*lokadhamma*) means phenomena whose nature is to disintegrate.
As to what that is, he says: "the pentad of aggregates" (*khandhapañcaka*). Therefore he says: "For that," and so forth. "How do I make?"—in what manner do I make him a fool who does not understand?
Therefore he says: "For my," and so forth. And likewise he said: "The path has been declared by me to you," and so forth. "The three worlds have been spoken of."
Having said that, in order to explain it, he spoke the passage beginning with “I do not, monks.
The commentary on the Puppha Sutta is finished.
3. Commentary on the Phenapiṇḍūpama Sutta.
95. That which cannot be seized by fighting for some reason is called *ayujjhā*. "In the place of turning back" means at the place where the flow of water turns back.
"On account of coming downstream" (*anusotāgamane*); or the reading is "by coming downstream" (*anusotāgamanena*).
"Increasing gradually" means growing in various ways through the contact of small and large masses of foam that have arisen here and there.
"Having reached": having brought [it], one would carry it away. "One should examine by means of a cause": one should investigate with knowledge.
Having said, "What might that which is called 'essence' be?", he says, "It would simply dissolve and perish," showing the total absence of such a thing.
By this, he shows that even form (*rūpa*) breaks apart due to its lack of essence. For just as the lack of essence is established through impermanence (*aniccatā*), so too is it here.
Thus, since the lack of essence (*asāratā*) establishes impermanence (*aniccatā*), he said, "Even form...

is indeed without essence," meaning that here there is no self (*attā*)—which would be the owner, the resident, the agent, and the controller—that exists under its own power; for there is no permanent essence, no stable essence, and no enduring essence. "It" refers to the mass of foam.
Even when grasped by means [of effort], it does not accomplish that purpose because it is unworthy of it. It is composed of many joints.
Having been formed in such and such a way;
even a fathom’s depth nowadays by the standard of human beings. It inevitably breaks apart when struck by waves.
When each individual drop of water falls. "The surface of the water" means the top of the water. A drop of water falling from elsewhere.
“Water-slime” (*udakajalla*) refers to the impurity of water that remains after it has become stagnant;
for by gathering that [impurity], one makes a film upon the water, and the designation “bubble” (*pubbuḷa*) applies to that film. “Basis” (*vatthu*) refers to the bases such as the eye and so forth.

“Object” (*ārammaṇa*) refers to objects such as visible forms and so forth. “Defilement-slime” (*kilesajalla*) refers to the stain of defilements, whether previously established or presently being acquired. “Contact-collision” (*phassasaṅghaṭṭana*)—
It is a convergence of contacts. It is like a bubble because its loveliness lasts but a moment.

For when, during the hot season, a mass of rays produced by the heat of the sun’s glare falls upon such a patch of ground, and the various types of elemental aggregates—consisting of atoms and their derivatives—arise here and there due to the force of winds blowing from all sides and whirl about, they are designated as "mirage. Therefore, it is entirely devoid of essence.
It is said: “Perception, too, is like a mirage in the sense of being without substance. And because it appears predominantly in the form of water to those who look at it, it is therefore said:
“to take and drink,” and so forth. “For the purpose of experiencing blue and so on” means for the purpose of experiencing an object such as blue and so on.
“It quivers” means that for a person whose craving has not been abandoned, it becomes as if it has attained a state of quivering.
It deceives a person who has not abandoned the perversion (vipallāsa). Therefore he said, “This is blue,” and so forth.
For from the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) comes the perversion of mind (citta-vipallāsa), and from that, the perversion of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa).
By “deceiving” means by the very act of apprehending the object in a distorted manner. For this apprehension occurs by way of distortion, namely, seeing what is actually not water as being water.
Having made a non-city into a city, there was the viewing of celestial musicians, dancers, and so forth.
"Kukkuka" refers to the stalk within all the leaf-sheaths of a plantain trunk;
thus he said, "of a kind not produced with a stalk," meaning that no dense stalk has developed within. "It is not so" means that it does not serve the purpose for which it was brought.
It exists. "Diverse characteristics" means diverse natures. "The aggregate of formations" refers to that which is called a single aggregate of formations.
"Of him" means of the person. "Free from the defects of cataracts and pustules" means free from both the defect of cataracts and the defect of pustules.
"Capable of seeing the essencelessness of what is without essence" means capable of seeing the state of being without essence in that which lacks essence. "Ephemeral" means of short duration.
It does not endure for long; therefore, it is said to have "a quick manifestation.

Furthermore, the statement that "the mind at the time of coming is indeed different" is spoken only in a gross sense. For in a single moment of a finger-snap (*accharakkhaṇa*), hundreds of thousands of millions of minds arise and cease.
A form displayed by an illusionist is called an "illusion. This refers to anything whatsoever, such as a skull, a brick, a stone, or sand.
"Deceives" means it deceives by taking what is not gold for gold, or what is not a pearl for a pearl, and so forth. But surely perception (*saññā*) also deceives and misleads, like a mirage;
and this consciousness (*viññāṇa*) also deceives like an illusion—so what is the distinction between these two?
Their literal meaning is common to both. Nevertheless, perception causes one to grasp at water where there is no water at all.
By making what is not a person appear as a person, it is of narrow scope due to its deceptive nature;
however, consciousness, by displaying whatever lacks that intrinsic nature as having it, is of great scope like an illusion. Therefore he said, "Whatever it may be," and so forth.
"In this way too" means that it is similar to an illusion even by virtue of its extremely rapid transformation.
"Taught": it was taught in this way by means of similes such as the lump of foam and so forth.
"Bhūri" refers to the earth; because his wisdom is like the earth in its quality of being subtle and its quality of being vast, he is called "Bhūripañña.
Therefore, he said, "By one of subtle wisdom," and so on. In the phrase "of swarms of worms, etc.," the word "etc. includes many vultures and other such creatures.
“Paveṇī” means a succession of teachings. “Bālalāpinī” refers to such expressions as “I,” “mine,” and so forth.

It breaks apart only after taking up the remaining elements (dhātus), because they arise together and cease together, and because it serves as the supporting condition for the physical basis (vatthurūpa); thus, it is not mentioned separately as “this.
“Vadhabhāvato” means because of the existence of killing, that is, death. “Saraṇaṃ” means a refuge or resort.
The commentary on the *Phenapiṇḍūpama-sutta* is finished.
4–6. Commentary on the *Gomayapiṇḍa-sutta* and others, verses 96–98.
They are called "eternal" (*sassatiyo*) because they exist forever, for all time, until the end of the eon; these are Sineru and the other [great mountains]. By means of them...
*Samam* means at the same time. *Anena* refers to the Blessed One. In the phrase *na yidam*, the letter *y* is used for euphonic junction (*padasandhi*);
*idam* is a particle (*nipātapada*). However, whatever it is connected with, it takes on the gender of that [noun]; thus it is said, "this dwelling in the holy life of the path.
Having stated, "it would not be discerned," the passage beginning with "for the path" is spoken in order to clarify that meaning. *Vivaṭṭento* means while turning away [from saṃsāra].
"Turning back" means causing non-occurrence.
"Royal capital" (*rājadhānī*) refers to the city where the king resides. "Made of thread" means made of strips of cloth in various colors.
The commentary on the section concerning the balls of cow dung and the thread is finished.
7. Commentary on the Gaddulabaddha Sutta 99.

Regarding the phrase "at which time the great ocean... (*yaṃ mahāsamuddo*): here, *yaṃ* is a reference to the occasion (*samaya*). Since this is a nominative case used in the sense of the locative, he says, "at which time" (*yasmiṃ samaye*).
And showing that this occasion is "coming" (*āyanti*), he says, "when the fifth sun has arisen."
I do not speak of a "delimitation" because the supreme knowledge of the Path (agga-magga-ñāṇa), which effects such delimitation, has not yet been attained.

Like a dog, the fool is dependent on the cycle of existence due to his nature of being subject to the taints (āsava). Like a tethered ox, he is bound by views. His personal existence (sakkāya) exists because of his nature of being subject to the taints.

Regarding the statement that "the worldling revolves within personal existence," this is an analytical description made by treating that [revolving] as distinct from the [mere] conventional expression "being" used for the continuity of the stream of existence.
The commentary on the Gaddulabaddha Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Second Gaddulabaddha Sutta. 100.
"Dependent upon the thicket of views" means dependent upon the thicket of views by way of such conditions as co-nascence and so forth; indeed, it is by depending [on them] that [the mind arises].
It proceeds because it is impossible to separate oneself from it.

"By the defilement of the mind alone" means by way of the mind being defiled through the ten bases of defilement (*kilesavatthu*). They "become bright" and "are purified" because the mind becomes clear through the attainment of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Taking "wandering mind" (*vicaraṇacitta*) as the subject, it is a wandering mind by virtue of its wandering. "Of the reckonings" (*saṅkhānāmā*) means those having such names.
“Brahmins and heretics” means: those who are Brahmins by birth, and those who wander about having adopted that sectarian mark (*pāsaṇḍa*) known as the ninety-eight sects.
“A cloth-merchant’s shop” means a shop for selling cloth. “Showing” means showing their state of mind according to the ripening of the karma of their respective destinies.
“Taking that mind” means taking up that mind which is like a cloth-merchant’s shop and wandering about. “Because it was done after reflecting.”
“‘The hands and feet of this form are thus, the face is thus, the proportions of the shape are thus,
the specific actions are thus, the distinctions of action are thus; the distinctions among the various beings must be made’—
having thought all this in such a way, and having performed it through the mind, including its purpose such as uprooting, casting down, setting in motion, and so forth.”

"Conceived by mind" means: the "mind seeking the means" is the consciousness that proceeds by way of the aforementioned means—such as "the hands and feet should be drawn thus"—and by way of the previously occurring means of preparing the ground, coloring, and correctly joining the pigments.
"Even more variegated than that" means even more variegated than that painting (*cittakamma*) by the painter.
Because none of the types of things merely thought about are actually produced through mental action (*cittakamma*). "By karmic mind" means by karmic consciousness (*kammaviññāṇa*).
Alternatively, "by karmic mind" means by the mind-nature of karma. It should be understood that this variegated nature of karma arises by way of craving (*taṇhā*).
This point has been elucidated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī-ṭīkā*. "Thus, minds" means thus, specific varieties of mind-forms (*cittarūpa*).
"It leads [beings] to a womb" means it causes them to reach various specific wombs, such as those born from eggs and so forth, just as a particular color [brings out the luster of] a crystal gem.
For it is not the specific karma—endowed with diverse potencies—that "leads to the womb";

rather, it serves as the condition for the arising of the respective result. The mental state of those beings is rooted in the womb; thus, whichever womb karma leads beings toward, that specific womb becomes their root.
This refers to the state of being variegated in mind among those beings. Therefore, he said, "having entered a womb," and so forth. "Of similar minds" means precisely having a state of similar mind.
The phrase beginning with "Thus" (*iti*) is a conclusion, presented in reverse order, of the very meaning already stated.

The passage beginning with "Moreover" (*apica*) is intended to show how, by way of the state of mind belonging to the animal realm, the mind itself is made to possess a particularly distinguished state of mind.
It has been stated. Therein, the connection is: "This so-called 'mind' (citta) should be understood as being even more variegated than that.

"By way of the variegated nature of co-nascent phenomena" means by way of the diversity of phenomena such as lust, faith, and so forth. "By way of the variegated nature of the planes" means by way of the variegated nature of the bases (adhiṭṭhāna).

"Those whose root cause is the diversity of kamma" means those for whom the diversity of kamma is the fundamental reason; [the text refers to] them. "The diversity of gender" is by way of the diversity of female gender and so forth.

And this should be understood by way of the diversity of their respective shapes. Diversity of perception (*saññānānatta*) is by way of the diversity of perceptions such as "woman," "man," "deity," "human," and so forth.
Diversity of designation (*vohāranānatta*) is by way of the diversity of designations such as "Tissa" and so on. Of minds (*cittānaṃ*) and variegated minds (*vicittānaṃ*).

Even that diversity of respective designations is made known by the mind alone. One is called a "dyer" (*rajako*) because one dyes cloth by means of producing colors from dye-stuffs, metals, and so forth.

The maker of beauty. The inclusion of the term "worldling" (puthujjana) is because the production of the material form designated as the individual body (attabhāva) by a worldling is certain and absolute.
The connection is made by supplying the words, “he produces beautiful form.
The commentary on the second Gaddulabaddha Sutta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Vāsijaṭa Sutta 101.
“Of the goal” means of welfare (*hita*). It is “not productive” because it was stated [in the preceding verse] as being for one who is not devoted to the practice of development (*bhāvanānuyoga*).
“The other” refers to the simile of the bright fortnight (*sukkapakkha*); it is “productive” because of being devoted to the practice of development. For that [development] belongs to him.

It should be understood as being more than that. "In the sense of possibility" means in the sense of the possibility of the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*). For it is in this way that the inclusion of the word *api* (even/also) is justified even in the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*). Alternatively, "in the sense of possibility" means in the sense of supposition.
When a meaning to be reckoned is stated without restriction, the particle *vā* (or) must be stated to express that unrestricted sense; thus, "eight or," and so forth, was said.
“Deficient or excessive” means that although they may be either deficient or excessive, one must grasp the single definitive sense;
thus it is said, “eight, ten, or twelve. With reference to this statement, the phrase “for the sake of the elegance of the expression,” and so forth, was spoken.
They are properly placed upon [the head] without being disturbed by the tips of the toenails. “Heat” (utu) refers to warm heat by way of bodily temperature.
Therefore he said, "made warm. "Cultivated" means perfumed by the incubation of a hen.
Having practiced this heedfulness by performing the three kinds of actions, such as sitting properly upon them; "to emerge safely" means to depart from there without obstacle.
Now, explaining that meaning, he said, "For they," and so forth. "Themselves" refers to the eggs. "Are matured" means fully ripened.
"Suitability for going forth" means fitness for departing from the world.

"That" refers to the application of the simile. "In this way" means by the manner that is now being stated. "By its meaning" means by way of the meaning of the thing to which the simile is applied (*upameyya*).
Having "harmonized" means having properly joined them together. The sharpness and other qualities of knowledge should be understood by way of the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).
For knowledge (ñāṇa), by its very nature and because it is accompanied by mindfulness, there is sharpness; by way of concentration, there is clarity;
by way of faith, there is serenity; and by way of energy, there is maturity. The "time of maturity" refers to the time of powerful insight (vipassanā).
The "time of increase" refers to the time of insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). For at the stage of conformity (anuloma), insight has already conceived the embryo.
It is so called because at that time the "womb of the path" (*maggagabbha*) has been taken up. *Tajjātikaṃ* means suitable for that practice of insight (*vipassanā*).
The Teacher also strikes and causes the breaking of the eggshell of ignorance (*avijjaṇḍakosa*) with this verse.
*Olambakasaṅkhātaṃ* means designated as the *Olambaka Sutta*. *Pala* is the name of that sutta. *Dhāretvā* means having memorized.
Having brought [the tools] for the purpose of knowing which wood is to be discarded and so forth. "One who removes the tumor of wood" is a *palagaṇḍa*;
by this, it is shown that in the latter phrase, the term *palagaṇḍa* is explained through the elision of the latter member (*uttarapadalopa*) of the compound *gaṇḍahāra*.
"In the place of grasping" means in the place where it is to be grasped with the hand. "By means of this, bodily misconduct and so forth are properly cast away"—this is the brief explanation.
By that [means]: for the person who is devoted to insight (vipassanā), the daily exhaustion of the taints (āsava) is what is intended here as the "benefit of insight.
By means of the winter season—this instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative; thus, the meaning is "in the winter season.
"They subside" means they become results of subsided activity. Therefore he said: "they become putrid."
The Dispensation is like the great ocean because of its inherent profundity. The practitioner of yoga is like a ship because of his crossing over the great flood.
"As if being consumed" means as if being completely exhausted by water, like a snail being eaten by a crab.
"Thinness" refers to a state of weakness due to the inability to give rise to the obsessions (*paryavasthāna*).
