"By means of the rapture and gladness born of insight-knowledge" means by means of the rapture and gladness arising from insight-knowledge.
"While it is being lifted up and fanned away" means while it is being lifted up by various modes of practice and fanned away by the contemplation of reflection.
Its weakness is illustrated by the statement: "The fetters are easily subsided; they become rotten."
The commentary on the Vāsijaṭa Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Anicca-saññā Sutta 102.
"While developing": this refers to the perception that arises in one who is developing the path through insight. Therefore he said: "All..."
"...it completely consumes sensual lust," and so forth. "Having extended" means having stretched out and spread over the entire field of cultivation.

"Defilements" refers to the various types of defilements (*upakkilesa*). "By means of the knowledge of the perception of impermanence" means by means of the knowledge accompanied by the perception of impermanence.
"Gathering" means that the knowledge of the perception of impermanence is like gathering, like leading away, and like stripping off. By this meaning...
By this meaning as stated in the text, the simile should be correlated: here, the one who gathers grass is like the practitioner (yogāvacara).

His satisfaction due to having performed his task there by means of gathering the grass and so forth is like this person’s spending of time in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) after having completely severed the defilements.
"They go to the peak" means they go to the peak by way of its far side. "By way of entering the peak" means by way of entering through the opening at the top of the peak.
"Having converged" means having converged by way of not entering further into the opening and by way of remaining firmly fixed.
The perception of impermanence is like the peak because it serves as the root for the state of firm standing by way of the contemplation of impermanence.

The wholesome states of the four planes are like rafters because they are rooted in the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*). The peak is the top, because it is the primary cause for the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of all the rafters.

This same principle applies here as well to the statement "the perception of impermanence is the peak. The phrase "the perception of impermanence is mundane" is said with reference to the contemplation of the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññānupassanā*). [This occurs] when the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) has been attained by way of the contemplation of impermanence.
The perception that has arisen receives the designation "perception of impermanence"; thus it was said:

"Bhikkhus, the perception of impermanence, when developed and cultivated, completely consumes all lust for sensual pleasures," and so forth. For likewise, in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, perception (*saññā*) is also mentioned in such passages as:
"At whatever time one develops supramundane perception," and so on. "In all similes" refers to the similes of the root-continuum and so forth.

Regarding the five similes: by the first—the similes of the farmer, the reed-thicket, the grass-blade, and the cluster of mangoes—the function of the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) is stated;

for by way of the expressions "uprooting," "pulling out," "crushing," "cutting down," "reaping," and "severing the stalk," the cutting off of the opposing factors by means of the perception of impermanence is demonstrated.
By the latter [similes], its power is shown, because the overwhelming of the opposing factors is made manifest.
The commentary on the Discourse on the Perception of Impermanence is finished.
The commentary on the Flower Chapter is finished.
The Middle Fifty [Discourses] is completed.
11. The Chapter on Extremes (Antavagga). 1. Commentary on the Sutta on Extremes (Antasuttavaṇṇanā). 103.
It is called an *anta* because it goes (*eti*) or proceeds by way of being mutually unassociated; thus he says, "Extremes means portions."

Regarding the phrase “the end of identity-cessation” (*sakkāyanirodhanta*), it is stated, “having applied the five aggregates by way of the Four Noble Truths,” because the condition for cessation has been grasped.
“The end” (*anta*)... [and so on] ...is stated according to the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), because the teaching of the Suttantas follows the natural order.
The commentary on the *Antasutta* is finished.
2–3. Commentary on the *Dukkhasutta* and others. 104–105.
Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the second also": it has the sense of inclusion. By this, he indicates that it is not only the first sutta, but the second as well.
With the words "and likewise the third," he concludes by stating: "having applied the five aggregates according to the four truths."
The commentary on the *Dukkhasutta* and others is finished.
4. Commentary on the *Pariññeyyasutta* 106.

Regarding the term "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*), there are here three kinds of full understanding: full understanding as knowledge (*ñātapariññā*), full understanding as investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*), and full understanding as abandonment (*pahānapariññā*).

Among these, full understanding through direct knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) exists solely for the sake of full understanding through scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*); and full understanding through scrutinization exists solely for the sake of full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*).
In this context, demonstrating the purpose by way of showing the function of the highest form of full understanding, he says:

"That which is to be fully understood" means that which is to be thoroughly known and transcended; the meaning is "that which is to be abandoned. Therefore the Blessed One said: "And what, bhikkhus, is full understanding?"
"The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. Therefore, they "surpass" it;
that is, they surpass the means for abandoning [the defilements]. "Standing having surpassed" means standing having abandoned; this is the meaning here.
The commentary on the *Pariññeyya-sutta* is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the Samaṇasutta, etc., 107–112.
The four truths have been explained because the origin and so forth of gratification and so forth have been taught.
The abandoning of defilements has been explained because the abandoning of lust has been illuminated.
The commentary on the Samaṇasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Antavagga is finished.
12. The Dhammakathikavagga.
1–2. Commentary on the *Avijjāsutta* and others.

113–114. *Yāvatā* means "because. *Samannāgato imāya... pe...* means "endowed with the delusion of ignorance (*avijjā*), which has the nature of non-knowing regarding the four noble truths, as described by the method beginning: 'He does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering. " *Samannāgato* means possessed of the confusion of that ignorance.
“By this much”: by this reason, one who has entered into, become possessed of, or approached ignorance, is said to be “endowed with ignorance.

“In the second [sutta] as well” refers to the *Vijjā-sutta*. He says, “The same method applies,” because the distinction is that in that case the teaching is given by way of clear knowledge (*vijjā*).
The commentary on the *Avijjā-sutta* and the others is finished.
3. Commentary on the Dhammakathikasutta 115.
By the first [verse], the preacher of the Dhamma (*dhammakathika*) is described, because it says, "he teaches the Dhamma.

By the second, the stage of the trainee (*sekha*) is described, because it says, "he is practicing. By the third, the stage of the non-trainee (*asekha*) is described, because it says, "he is liberated through non-clinging."

Because it was said: “...it happens. By the Blessed One, when questioned by the preacher of the Dhamma. “Having distinguished” means having distinguished and exalted him on account of his status as a preacher of the Dhamma.
“Two planes” refers to the plane of the trainee (*sekha*) and the plane of the one beyond training (*asekha*).
The commentary to the *Dhammakathika Sutta* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Second Dhammakathikasutta 116.
"Three answers" means three answers corresponding to the questions.
The commentary on the Second Dhammakathikasutta is finished.
5–9. Commentary on the *Bandhana-sutta* and others (117–121).
“Shore” (*tīra*) refers to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), taking it as the near shore. Therefore he said: “But this other generation runs only along the shore.

“The further shore” (*pāra*) refers to Nibbāna, taking it as the opposite shore of saṃsāra. “Bound” (*baddha*) means because the abandonment of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) has not been accomplished.
Bound by the fetter of defilements, even in the bright fortnight, it is stated that there is merely a negation of the fetters of form and so forth through the contemplation of views;

the intention is not that there is liberation. Since the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is discussed in this sutta—because of the passage, "One who sees the near shore and sees the far shore, him I call one liberated from suffering"—it can be said that the round and its unraveling (*vaṭṭavivaṭṭa*) are being explained.
The sixth and subsequent suttas have their meanings already explained, as they follow the method set forth below.
The commentary on the *Bandhanasutta* and others is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Sīlavantasutta*.
122. "In the sense of affliction" means in the sense of oppression and in the sense of causing pain from the very moment of its initial arising.
"In the sense of internal corruption" means in the sense of being corrupt and in the sense of being agitated within. "In the sense of digging up" means in the sense of tearing out.
"In the sense of suffering" means by way of the state of mere suffering. For in the world, suffering is called "aghā" (misery) because it strikes excessively. It is discordant.
...pe... "In the sense of condition" means by way of being the condition for the affliction produced by the primary elements that are dissimilar to the elements and so forth as they occur.
"In the sense of not belonging to a self" means because it is not subject to a self. "In the sense of disintegration" means in the sense of breaking up in various ways.
"In the sense of emptiness of a being" means in the sense of emptiness of a self designated as a "being. "By way of the absence of a self" means...
Because of the non-existence of a self imagined by those who hold wrong views. Regarding the phrase "empty of non-self," the word "from another" (*parato*) should be supplied here;
therefore, it should be stated as "non-attention due to two [reasons].
The commentary on the *Sīlavanta-sutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the Sutavantasutta 123.
Regarding the phrase "likewise the eleventh," the word "likewise" (*tathā*) here draws in the expression "is quite clear. "Here" (*idha*) refers to the eleventh [sutta].
Knowledge that arises by way of learning, retaining, practicing, and attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is [called] "learning of the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhānasuta*).
It is called "heard" because it has been accomplished.
The commentary on the *Sutavanta* Sutta is finished.
12–13. Commentary on the *Kappa* Sutta and others.
124–125. "Similar to the Rāhulovāda" means similar to the suttas found in the Rāhulovāda Sutta.
The commentary on the Kappa Sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Dhammakathika Vagga is finished.
13. The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga). 1–10. Commentary on the Suttas beginning with "Of the Nature of Arising" (Samudayadhammasutta), §§126–135.
Regarding this Chapter on Ignorance: only the Four Noble Truths are discussed; therefore, the intention is that [the meaning] is self-evident because it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the Samudayadhamma-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Avijjāvagga is finished.
14. The Kukkuḷavagga.
1–14. Commentary on the Kukkuḷasutta and others (136–149).

A great mass of embers with fire within; there, because it burns upwards and downwards as one treads upon it, consuming everything up to the very tips of the hair, it is called *kukkuḷa*—that which burns badly (*kucchitaṃ kuḷati*).
However, form, feeling, and so forth, burn for only a certain period of time even more than that.

And because it is like hot embers in the sense of being a great conflagration, it is called *kukkuḷa*. "The characteristics of impermanence, etc. refers to the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
The commentary on the *Kukkuḷa-sutta* and others is finished.
The commentary on the *Kukkuḷa-vagga* is finished.
15. Diṭṭhivagga 1–9.
Commentary on the Ajjhattasutta and following (150–158).
“Having made a condition” means having made the condition of dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*). By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), wrong view, personality-view, and self-view are included.
It includes the fetters (*saññojana*), adherences (*abhinivesa*), bondages (*vinibandha*), and clingings (*ajjhosāna*). Among these, the adherences are craving, conceit, and views.
The bondages are the mental bondages mentioned in such passages as "he is not free from lust for the body. The clingings are the clingings of craving and views.
The remaining terms are easily understood.
The commentary on the Ajjhatta-sutta and others is finished.
10. Commentary on the Ānanda-sutta. 159.
"At the time of his living" means at the time of his being alive. "Not seeing [any] abandoning"—it is said that the Elder had affection for the Blessed One.
"Exceedingly. "I will seize the mind; I will win over the mind. One must go [to the teacher], therefore it is "with impediments.

"Gladdening the mind" means awakening the mind. Liberation... [as before] ...is "pertaining to penetration" because it serves as a condition for future realization, but it is not so called at that moment because it does not yet bring about a specific distinction.
The commentary on the Ānanda Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Diṭṭhi Vagga is finished.
The Upper Fifty is completed.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the Khandha Saṃyutta of the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the Commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, is completed. 2.
The *Rādha Saṃyutta*.
1. First Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Māra Sutta. 160.
Showing that this word "Māra" is a noun denoting a state (bhāvasādhana), [the text says]: "Or it may be 'one who causes death' (mārayati), thus it would be 'death' (maraṇaṃ)."
He said: "Māretā" means one who must die; because one must go toward death (maraṇa), he said "māretabbo.
"For the sake of Nibbāna without clinging" means that the state of an Arahant—known as the liberation from the fruit—is precisely for the sake of Nibbāna without clinging.
"Within the interior of Nibbāna" means within the attainment of Nibbāna without clinging; it is only with reference to that [attainment] that this path and holy life (brahmacariya) are lived.
There is nothing beyond that. "Assa" means of the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
The commentary on the *Māra-sutta* is finished.
2–10. Commentary on the *Satta-sutta* and others.
161–169. *Laggapucchā* means a question concerning attachment (*lagga*), that is, being bound.

If a "being" (*satta*) is so called because of the state of being attached (*satta*) to form and so forth, how can those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) be called beings? [The answer is: because they were previously beings.

*Kīḷāvigama* means the removal or cessation of play. Because it leads one along the continuity of existence (*bhava-pabandha*) like a mechanical rope, craving (*taṇhā*) is called the "rope of existence" (*bhavarajjū*).
The commentary on the Seven Suttas, etc., is finished.
The commentary on the First Chapter is finished.
2. The Second Chapter.
1–12. Commentary on the *Mārasutta* and others (170–181).

There is no such thing as death apart from form and the other aggregates; the designation "death" applies only to the dissolution of form and the rest. The nature of death is the state of destruction.
The commentary on the *Mārasutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Second Chapter is finished.
3–4. The Chapter on Entreaties, etc. 1–11.
Commentary on the Eleven Suttas beginning with "Māra," etc.

182–205. A subtle cause manifests; therefore, this Elder was placed at the head of those who possess ready wit (*paṭibhāneyyaka*). This was by way of the qualities that ripen liberation (*vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma*), and not by way of having attained penetration (*paṭivedha*).
The commentary on the group of eleven suttas beginning with the *Māra* Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the group of suttas beginning with the *Āyācana* Vagga is finished.
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscure in the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya entitled the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, specifically the Exposition of the Rādha-Saṃyutta, is completed. 3.
The Diṭṭhi-Saṃyutta (Connected Discourses on Views).
1. The Chapter on Stream-Entry (Sotāpattivagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Winds (Vātasuttavaṇṇanā) 206.
"These are not winds"—those things which break tree branches and so forth are called "winds" only because they belong to the category of beings; they are not [inherently] winds.
They are indeed permanent, stable, and eternal. Therefore he said, "But the wind," and so forth. By this, he refers to the fourth body among the seven bodies.
This so-called "wind-element" is that which breaks tree branches and the like; the meaning is that it is similar to wind.
With the phrase "like a pillar in a desert," he shows its state of being motionless; with "like a mountain peak," however, he shows that it remains for all eternity.

For this wind, having adhered to the impermanence of the body, persists with the thought, "Let there not be another [state] through impermanence," and thus it oppresses [the body] by saying, "The winds do not blow.
This same method applies to such phrases as "the rivers flow" and so forth. But as for "water," he says this with reference to the second body.
However, the fetus does not emerge, because it is obtained precisely through its state of being fixed like a peak and so on. They do not rise up at all, just as...
"O winds, because the world thus stands [in dependence], it is merely a mental construct"—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the Vāta-sutta is finished.
2–4. Commentary on the Etaṃmama-sutta and others.
207–209. The visible object-base (*rūpāyatana*) is "seen" because it is to be seen by the eye. The sound-base (*saddāyatana*) is "heard" because it is to be heard by the ear.
The three bases beginning with odor (*gandhāyatana*), which grasp what is present, are "cognized" (*muta*) because they are to be apprehended by the nose and so forth after reaching [their objects].
The remaining seven bases, beginning with the eye, are called "cognized" (*viññāta*) because they are to be known solely by mental consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). Thus it is said: "attained."
"Attained" (*anuppatta*) means that whatever is to be reached has been attained after having been sought and searched for.
"Sought" (*pariyesita*) means what was sought out. "Mentally traversed" (*cittena anusañcarita*) means what was thought over by the mind.
Having shown that a fourfold permutation is possible within these two terms, "attained" and "sought," he explains the terms *patta* (attained) and *pariyesita* (sought) according to that permutation.
Then, in order to show what has been mentally investigated and brought forth, the passage beginning with “In the world indeed... was stated.

Therein, that which is "obtained after seeking" is so called because it is the state of being grasped through the act of seeking. That which is "merely sought" is so called by taking it to mean simply the act of seeking itself;
this is because [the text] speaks of what is mentally investigated as being obtained after seeking. In the first alternative, there would be confusion.
The phrase beginning with “Alternatively” was stated in order to show that [the object] exists without confusion. “All” refers to the cognized (viññāta) and so forth;
for since these are apprehended by mental consciousness (manoviññāṇa), they are said to be “mentally scrutinized” (manasā anuvicarita), and are not seen, heard, or sensed.
The commentary on the *Etam-mama-sutta* and others is concluded.
5. Commentary on the *Natthidinnasutta* 210.
Regarding the statement, "‘Given’ refers to giving under the heading of the object to be given," he says: "With reference to the non-existence of the fruit of what is given.
But how can they reject the actual substance that has been given, such as food and so forth? This same method applies to the phrase "sacrificed" (*yiṭṭha*) and "offered" (*huta*).
*Mahāyāga* is a great offering common to all. *Paheṇakasakkāra* is the hospitality that should be rendered to guests.
*Phala* refers to both the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*nissandaphala*). *Vipāka* is the fruit of correspondence (*sadisaphala*).

Regarding the phrase "for one staying in the next world this world does not exist": for one situated in the next world, this world—which is to be obtained through karma—does not exist. In this world...
"Even for one who stands [in this world], there is no other world": for one standing in this world, an other world to be attained through karma does not exist.
He states the reason for this: "All are cut off right there, right then.
These beings, wherever they stand—in whatever existence, womb, or other state—are cut off right there; they perish by way of non-arising and dissolution.
"By way of the absence of fruit" means that they say "there is no mother, there is no father" on account of the absence of fruit for right or wrong conduct toward one's parents;

it is not because of the non-existence of the parents themselves, nor because of the absence of honor or dishonor currently being performed toward them, since they are directly perceptible in the world. The arising of these beings is like that of a bubble.
He said, "There are no spontaneously born beings," in order to show that there is no prior instance of anyone having come here after falling away from existence elsewhere. [The opponent] replied:
"A true ascetic, knowing things as they really are, ought to remain restrained without speaking of anything; otherwise, it would be mere boasting."

For what can one person do for another? Likewise, there would be no support whatsoever for the accomplishment of one's own welfare, as it would be cut off right there and then; thus he said, "Those who... [etc. ...proclaim this.
That which is connected with the four great elements is "composed of the four great elements" (*cātumahābhūtiko*). Just as a vessel produced from clay—
Just as a [vessel] made of clay [is produced from its causes], so too this [body] is produced from the four great elements; thus he said, "composed of the four great elements.
"The internal earth element" refers to the earth element existing within the continuum of a sentient being. "The external earth element" refers to the great external earth.
"It follows along" means it moves or proceeds in accordance with that [earth element]. "It approaches" means [it proceeds] from the external mass of earth previously [mentioned].
The earth that constitutes a portion of that [cosmic mass], having arrived and attained an internal state, was established as a sentient being;

now, like the earth of a jar or other objects, it approaches—that is, goes toward—that very same external body of earth. The meaning is that it becomes entirely indistinguishable from it and attains a state of oneness.
The same method applies to water and the other elements as well; in this context, by means of Pajjunna (the rain god), from the great ocean...
Just as rainwater that has been taken up returns again to the great ocean, or as the heat known as fire that was taken up by the rays of the sun returns again to the solar ray,

or as a great wind that has issued from a mass of air returns to that very same mass of air, so the one who holds such a view (*diṭṭhigatika*) himself contradicts his own position. For it is like the case of a madman’s turban.
This is the demonstration of those who hold to wrong views. He says that the sense-faculties, with the mind as the sixth, "leap into space" because their objects are of the nature of space;
for by the mention of the subject (the faculty), the objects are indeed already included.

"Parts characterized by virtue and non-virtue" means portions consisting of merits and defects. "The body itself is the parts" is what is intended, because it is through the body that various actions are to be accomplished.
"Those who give (dattu) are those who are deluded (muyhanti); thus, they are deluded persons (mūḷhapuggalā). It was prescribed by those deluded, foolish people.
The commentary on the *Natthidinnasutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Karotīsutta*.
211. *Sahatthā karontassā* means "of one who acts with his own hand.

Here, even the *nissaggiya-thāvara* (forfeiture regarding fixed objects) and other rules are included under the category of acting with one's own hand. *Hatthādīni* refers to the hands, feet, ears, nose, and so forth.
Regarding "cooking, burning, and afflicting," he says "of one who presses with a stick. In the *Papañcasūdanī*, the meaning "of one who threatens" is stated; however, here—
Just as in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, having restrained that person with a reprimand as if with a staff, it is said: "of one who oppresses with a staff.
"Causing grief for oneself" means causing for oneself the reason for another's grief, or producing grief [in another]. "By others who act according to one's word.
"One who himself stirs" means by means of the exertion of harming another, he himself also...

"Phandato" (from one who is moving). Regarding the word "atipātayato" (of one who causes to fall), it functions both in the sense of a simple agent and in the sense of a causal agent; thus he says: "even of one who kills, and even of one who causes another to kill.
"By way of cause" means by way of causing [another] to act. A house-joint is that which stands connected on both the inside and the outside of a wall. Without leaving anything behind...
“Niravaseso” means the complete removal; thus it is “nillopo. That which is practiced in a single house is “vilopo,” and one who practices it is an “ekāgāriko.
Killing on a path in every way is “paripantho. Evil is not produced because it was non-existent previously and cannot be brought into being;
therefore, there is no evil. If this is so, how is it that beings engage in evil? To this he says: “But beings have the perception, ‘We are acting.’”
"May they be so"—thus it occurs to him: "Indeed, for these beings, actions such as violence do not touch the self, because of its permanence and its immutability;
the body, however, is insentient, like a piece of wood or a block of stone, and even when it is destroyed, there is no evil whatsoever.
*Khuranemīhi*: with wheels having rims made of sharpened blades; the meaning is "with rims resembling razor blades."
With the intention that the southern direction along the Ganges is an unsuitable location while the northern direction is a suitable location, he said, “Even if [he goes] to the south,” and so forth;
thus he stated, “The people on the southern bank are harsh,” and so on. “A great sacrifice” (mahāyāga) means a great sacrifice similar to the Mahāvijita sacrifice.
“By the observance of the Uposatha” (uposathakammena): here, the word *ca* (and) is indicated by elision.

For the word *dama* here is intended to signify both restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and the Uposatha precept (*uposathasīla*). Some, however, say that the phrase "by the Uposatha rite" is a qualification of the taming of the senses;
thus they explain the meaning as "by the taming of the senses which constitutes the Uposatha rite.
"By the restraint of virtue" means by the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*). "By truthful speech" means by true speech (*saccavācā*).
It is mentioned separately because it is regarded in the world as a merit of greater weight.

For just as false speech is the gravest among unwholesome qualities, so is truthful speech the gravest among wholesome qualities. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Of one who has transgressed a single quality," and so forth.
"Occurrence" (pavatti) refers to its functioning as the condition for the production of a fruit within the continuum of one who is said to be the doer.
The Sabbathā section rejects action in every possible way, as stated in the passage beginning with "for one who acts.
The commentary on the *Karoto-sutta* is finished.
7. Commentary on the *Hetu-sutta*.

212. "By both" means by the statement that negates the condition of cause (*hetu-paccaya*). "Condition of defilement" (*saṃkilesa-paccaya*) is the cause for the state of being defiled, the state of being stained.
"Condition of purification" (*visuddhi-paccaya*) is the cause for purification, for cleansing from defilement.
"There is no power" means that there is no so-called power among beings that brings about success in this present life, in future lives, or the attainment of *nibbāna*.
There is nothing [else]. Therefore he said, “In which,” and so forth. This is merely an illustration; for this [term] also excludes that which is defiled (*saṃkilesika*).
They are synonyms for one another: in the sense of being abundant in a particular action it is *bala* (strength);

in the sense of bringing about the state of being brave and heroic it is *vīriya* (energy); and because it must be exercised by one who bears the human burden through a firm grasp of that very [energy], it is *purisathāma* (manly power).
It should be understood that "manly exertion" (*purisaparakkama*) is said because of the process of ascending to ever-higher states.
They are called "beings" (*satta*) because of their connection with existence (*sat*), or because they are attached (*satta*) to form and the other aggregates;

they are called "living beings" (*pāṇa*) because of their breathing through the process of inhalation and exhalation. Having classified them according to their possession of one faculty and so forth, he says "one-facultied" (*ekindriya*), etc. [Regarding] the eggshell and so forth...

Because they come into being (*bhavana*), they are called "beings" (*bhūta*); thus he says, "They say... pe ...egg-born. Because they live, like those who sustain their breath, and because they grow, they are called "living beings" (*jīva*);
this is what the Sāliya and others assert. They have no mastery (*vasa*) over defilement or purification;

thus they are "without mastery" (*avasā*). They have no strength or vigor; thus they are "weak" (*abalā*) and "lacking vigor" (*avīriyā*). Their state is fixed (*niyatata*); they are like threads that cannot be cut or jewels that cannot be broken.
"Fixedness" (niyama) refers to the necessity of proceeding in a determined manner according to the destiny, birth, bondage, and liberation [of beings].
"Going here and there" means approaching various destinies by way of the six classes of noble birth (*abhijāti*). "Conjunction" (*saṅgati*) is a coming together through a combination.

"It is simply the intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvo eva*) means, for example, the sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of wood-apple fruits (*kapittha*), or [the specific characteristics] of beasts and birds.

The state of having various mental forms—thus, the transformation of the entire world in such and such ways without causes and conditions—is simply its inherent nature (sabhāva), which is unconditioned (akittima).
Therefore he said, "By which," and so forth. The six classes of beings (chaḷabhijātiyo) will be explained in detail later.
Those who say that they experience both pleasure and pain [deny] the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (adukkhamasukha-bhūmi) in every respect.
By pointing out that "they do not know," he said, "showing that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain.
The commentary on the *Hetusutta* is finished.
8–10. Commentary on the *Mahādiṭṭhisutta*, etc.
213–215. *Akatā* means not made by anyone, whether by an even or uneven cause.
They are called *akatavidhānā* because they have no maker, no agent, and no arrangement. By these two phrases, he shows that in the world they are not produced by any cause or condition.
*Na nimmitā iddhiyā pi* means not fashioned even by the psychic power of any possessor of such power, such as a deity or a Brahmā.
Or they are not even created by supernormal power (*iddhi*). "Uncreated" (*animmita*) means that they do not cause anyone to create.

By the term "unproducers" (*ajanaka*), he rejects the notion that the earth-element and so forth possess the quality of producing matter and other phenomena. For his view is that visible forms, sounds, and so forth exist independently of the earth-element and the rest.
Just as a mountain peak is neither produced by anyone nor does it produce anything for anyone, so too are these [elements].

He said: “Fixed as a peak. The intention is this: regarding that which is said, “the sprout and so forth arise from the seed and so forth,” it emerges from that [seed] only while already existing, not while non-existent;
otherwise, anything could arise from anything at all. “Stationed” means stationed in a state free from modification.
“Do not move” means they do not undergo modification. By virtue of the absence of modification...
For these seven bodies possess the stability of a pillar set in its base; they are immovable and remain fixed in their own nature.
Therefore, he said, "they do not undergo transformation. And because they have the quality of being non-transformable, they do not obstruct one another.
For if there were the possibility of inducing change, there might be obstruction; likewise, if there were the possibility of providing assistance, there might be assistance.
To show the absence of that [agent], the text says "not capable" (*nālam*) and so forth. Because it is merely earth and is a part of the body, it is called the "earth-body.
Since bodies—of which the living being is the seventh—are eternal and thus lack the capacity for transformation, they cannot be killed nor can they be caused to be slain;
therefore, there is no one at all who kills or causes to kill. Hence he said: "But only among the seven," and so on. If there is no one who kills, [how can there be killing?]
"How is it a 'blow from a weapon'? To this he said: "Just as in the case of a heap of beans," and so forth.

The intention is that there is merely a matter of perception, not actual killing and so on, because in the ultimate sense (paramattha) the seven constituent bodies (kāya) are incapable of being disturbed.
"Of those with prominent births" means those who, among humans, animals, and so forth, belong to the preeminent births such as Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, lions, tigers, and the like.
“Sixty hundreds” means six thousand. The phrase “and five hundred actions” is explained as “and five hundred actions.
By the words “this is the same method,” he refers back to this very point: that [the opponent] merely demonstrates a useless view through mere reasoning (*takkamatta*).
And here, by the term “merely through reasoning,” since logicians are unrestrained—
Regarding "speculation" (*parikappa*): whatever one has speculated about oneself, imagining it to be essential, they adhere to it as such and grasp at a speculative view (*takka-diṭṭhigāha*).
Therefore, he shows that wise people should not engage in investigation regarding their grounds for views.
"Some" refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery. For they [hold that] "the five faculties" are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

They say, "These five faculties they designate as 'the five actions'. Their doctrine is that because [bodily and vocal action] is coarse, it is the doctrine that they are "complete actions" (*paripuṇṇakamma*).
The construction is that because mental action is not coarse, it is the doctrine that it is "half an action" (*upaḍḍhakamma*).
When one should say "sixty-two ways of practice" (*dvāsaṭṭhipaṭipadā*), those who do not know the natural language [of Pali] say "sixty-two ways of practice" (*dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā*).
"In one" means in one *mahākappa*. And even there, it refers to one *asaṅkhyeyyakappa* known as the period of the world's expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi*).

"Sheep-slayers" (*orabbhika*) are those who kill sheep; in this same way, "pig-slayers" (*sūkarika*) and others are to be understood. "Hunters" (*ludda*) refers to anyone else such as deer-hunters, fowlers, and so forth;
they are called "of dark birth" (*kaṇhābhijāti*) because they are intent upon evil deeds. "Bhikkhus" refers to [those] in the Buddha’s dispensation.
The monks. It is said that they say, "They consume [the requisites] with desire and lust," meaning that they put thorns into the four requisites and eat them.
Why is that? Because they hold a wrong grasp, thinking that the monks partake of the most excellent requisites;
for even while consuming requisites obtained through right means, they act in opposition to the system of the Ājīvakas.
Others say that they are so called because they eat after having thrown [food] upon thorns.
Some are renunciants who are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification; for they behave as if they were living on thorns, and thus they are called "thorn-livers" (*kaṇṭakavuttika*).
They are exceedingly pure due to their observance of vows such as standing while eating and the prohibition against bathing.
"Acelaka-sāvakā" refers to the disciples of the Ājīvakas. It is said that because they firmly adhered to the Ājīvaka doctrine and the Ājīvaka tenets, they were even whiter (purer) than the Nigaṇṭhas.
Nanda and others, it is said, remained having brought such a practice of the Ājīvakas to its highest excellence;
therefore, they are described as being whiter than both the Nigaṇṭhas and the Ājīvaka disciples. "Born of the supreme Sukka lineage"—this is their tenet.
"Purisabhūmiyo" (the stages of men) is a designation by way of the person who exerts effort. Women also desire these stages;

"the monk and the one who has entered" (*pannaka*) and so forth is their very canonical text (*pāḷi*). Therein, "one who has entered" (*pannaka*) means one who wanders for alms, or one who has entered upon their practice.
"Jina" (the conqueror) means one who is worn out (*jiṇṇa*), having inferior elements due to old age, or one who has conquered the adversaries to his own practice.
Having conquered [the defilements], he stood firm. It is said that, being in such a state, he did not speak even the Dhamma to anyone. Therefore it is said: "He said nothing.
They say that even when someone performed an unpleasant act such as spitting at him, he said nothing because of his capacity for forbearance.
Regarding "one who does not obtain": this refers to the combination of causes for non-obtainment mentioned in the passage beginning, "He does not accept from the mouth of a jar," and so forth.
I did not obtain it. Therefore, because he was overcome by the weakness of hunger and devoted solely to his bed, they call such a recluse "one who has fallen to the ground.
"Hundreds of livelihoods" means hundreds of ways of life that constitute the livelihood of beings. By the mention of cattle, the species of sheep is included;

by the mention of deer, the entire species of wild animals such as the ruru-deer, gayal, and so forth is included. "Many gods" refers to those belonging to the realms of the Four Great Kings up to the Brahmakāyika gods.
There are many types of deities according to their internal divisions. Among them, some of the internal divisions of the Cātumahārājika gods should be illustrated by means of the Mahāsamaya Sutta.
Humans are also infinite; humans have infinite divisions based on distinctions such as continent, country, clan, lineage, and livelihood.
*Pesācā* are simply *pisācā*; these are the very large *ajagara-peta*s and so forth. They call the Chaddanta Lake and the Mandākinī by the names Kuḷīra and Mucalinda.
"Pavuṭā" means all kinds of knots. Even a wise person... [as before] ...does not go upward. Why? Because the time for the wandering of beings is fixed.
One "ripens" that which is unripened—the cause for wandering—by means of virtue and so forth, so that purity may be attained very quickly.
Having encountered and encountered that which is ripened karma, one exhausts it by bringing it to a state of full ripeness at the proper time.

"Name. "In a ball of thread" means on a coil of thread. "It runs away even as it is being unwound" shows by way of this simile that the saṃsāra of beings is exhausted through gradual progression and does not increase, because its form is limited.
It is said that the ball of thread goes even as it is being unwound; and that is only according to the measure of the thread—for when there is no more thread, where would it go?
“A ball of thread. Therefore he said: “When the thread is exhausted, it does not go on. The intention is that it remains right there at the end of the thread.
“By way of time”: having been wound upon oneself, pleasure and pain—being unwound according to the aforementioned time—the fool and the wise alike pass away; they go, but do not transcend saṃsāra.
The commentary on the Mahādiṭṭhisutta and others is finished.
11–18. Commentary on the Antavāsutta and others, 216–223.
"A sign developed on one side" means a kasiṇa sign developed on one flank. "By grasping" means by way of acquisition.

"Having seen with the eye of jhāna" means by way of grasping [the object]. "By reasoning" (*takkena*) means not by one who possesses [supernormal knowledge], but merely by means of reasoning (*takka-mattena*).

"A view has arisen" (*uppanna-diṭṭhi*) refers to the view that has arisen: "The world. "Increased on all sides" (*sabbato vaḍḍhitaṃ*) means the sign of the kasiṇa, which is immeasurable in every direction.

"Only one" (*ekameva*) refers to the view that has arisen: "There is only one basis" (*ekameva vatthu*). "The eighteen explanations" (*aṭṭhārasa veyyākaraṇāni*) refers to those that have attained the characteristics of an explanation (*veyyākaraṇa-lakkhaṇa*).
There are eighteen suttas. "One journey" means one journey of exposition.
The commentary on the *Antavā-sutta* and others is finished. 2.
Commentary on the Second Chapter on Journeys, etc. (*Dutiyagamanādivagga-vaṇṇanā*)
"Stated by way of suffering" means it was stated by way of suffering, beginning with: "Thus, monks, when there is suffering, it is by depending on suffering.
The second method of exposition (*veyyākaraṇa-gamana*) is exactly like that. Therefore he said: "In that case too, there are eighteen expositions.
"Together with those" means together with the expositions occurring in the manner beginning with "the self is possessed of form" (*rūpī attā hoti*). "That" refers to the second method of exposition.
"Only the object" means only the object known as the *kasiṇa*. By the word "speculator," the inclusion of pure rationalists (*suddhatakkika*) should be understood.
"By way of impermanence and suffering" means: "Whatever is impermanent is suffering; when that exists, based on that, such a view arises"—it is by way of this stated impermanence and suffering.
"By those very same" means by those very types mentioned in the second series (*peyyāla*).
"By way of three turnings" means that it was spoken by those same twenty-six suttas in the fourth peyyāla by way of three turnings; such is the construction.
The commentary on the Second Chapter, beginning with the "Gamanavagga," is finished.
[From] the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, the commentary on the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) of the Commentary on the *Diṭṭhisaṃyutta* is completed.
4. The *Okkantasaṃyutta*: 1–10.
Commentary on the Discourses on the Eye, etc. (*Cakkhusuttādivaṇṇanā*).
302–311. *Saddhādhimokkha* means resolution proceeding by way of faith, not resolution proceeding merely by way of conviction.
*Dassana* (vision) is also rightness (*sammatta*). That certainty which proceeds by way of that [vision] is *sammattaniyāma*, namely the Noble Path.
It indicates the state of being without obstacle because it proceeds as an antidote to the destruction of the eon. Thus he said: "Therefore it was said," and so forth.

By "Kappasīsa," he refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). For that [world] burns away; it is not the eon (*kappa*) itself, but the time of burning is the time of the meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
"A stable eon" means a fixed eon (*ṭhitakappa*); one who possesses such an eon is "one for whom the eon is stable" (*ṭhitakappī*), meaning one capable of establishing the eon.
"Beholding" (*olokana*) is vision (*dassana*) characterized by the realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*). They "endure" (*khamanti*) or "bear" (*sahanti*), meaning they understand (*ñāyanti*).
The commentary on the Cakkhu-sutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Okkanta-saṃyutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Uppāda-saṃyutta.
312–321. All is indeed manifest because there is nothing new [to be explained].
The commentary on the *Uppāda-saṃyutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Kilesa-saṃyutta*.
322–331. This is desire-and-lust (*chanda-rāga*) regarding the eye. It is called a secondary defilement (*upakkilesa*) because it defiles by approaching.
Regarding the word "of the mind" (*cittassa*), the accuser, not accepting it as a general term, asked: "Of which mind? The other replied with the following intention:

"Granted that there is no secondary defilement for the supramundane mind in the sense of causing torment or producing a state of sluggishness, yet there certainly is one in the sense of obstructing its arising. Thus he spoke.

Regarding the phrase “of the mind belonging to the four planes,” the accuser clarifies his own intention with the words “belonging to the three planes” and so forth, while the other [respondent] does so with the words “because of the prevention of arising” and so forth.
It is called renunciation (*nekkhamma*) because it has emerged from all defilements through its occurrence by way of the subsiding and abandoning of the noble fruits;
however, the state of renunciation in the case of the Path and Nibbāna is taken here in its highest sense.
He said: "Inclined toward renunciation" means inclined toward the nine supramundane states (*navalokuttaradhamma*). "Having fully known" means having known by way of direct confrontation.

"Among those things to be realized" means among those things to be made manifest through direct perception. "The sixfold states of direct knowledge" refers to the states associated with the noble path (*ariyamagga*).
The commentary on the *Kilesasaṃyutta* is concluded.
7. Sāriputta Saṃyutta 1–9.
Commentary on the Vivekaja Sutta and others, 332–340.
Regarding the phrase "it is not thus": here, let there be no thought, "I am attaining [absorption]," or "I have attained [absorption]."
At that time, it is because of the absence of such mental application (*ābhoga*). But why does the thought "I have emerged" not occur?
It simply does not occur at all, because the conceit of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) has been entirely abandoned.
The commentary on the *Vivekaja-sutta* and others is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Sūcimukhīsutta 341.

Regarding the phrase "when that statement was rejected": when the statement spoken by the female wanderer, "You eat with your face turned downwards," was rejected [by the Blessed One] with the words, "Indeed, sister, I do not," they raised an objection (*vāda*).
"With face turned upwards" (*ubbhamukho*) means with face turned toward the upper direction. "The eastern direction, etc."... [text fragment]
The four cardinal directions; the four intermediate directions beginning with the southeast.
*Vatthuvijjā* is the science connected with the preparation of the ground and the sowing of seeds in relation to monasteries, sites for monasteries, and so forth.
To demonstrate its nature as a wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*), the passage beginning with "of those" (*tesaṃ*) was stated. [This refers to] those respective donors who provide one's own requisites.
“Going here and there” means traveling from one village to another or to distant regions for the purpose of carrying their message.

“Thus he reported” means that, having heard the Elder’s discourse on the Dhamma— which was free from self-praise and disparagement of others, pleasant to the ear, lovely, and heart-stirring— the people, with minds full of faith,
reported to the families these words praising the virtues of the Dispensation, beginning with, “The Sakyan-son ascetics are righteous.”
The commentary on the Sūcimukhī Sutta is finished.
The commentary on the Sāriputta Saṃyutta is finished.
8. The Nāga Saṃyutta.
1. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta 342.
"Born from an egg" means born from an egg. "Born from a womb" means born within the amniotic sac known as the *vatthikoṣa*, which is the membrane of the placenta.
"Born from moisture" means arisen in a moist or damp place. "As if having arrived by transformation" means produced as if not having descended from anywhere at all.
"Of persons" means of those persons who are to be trained in such a way.
The commentary on the *Suddhikasutta* is finished.
2–50. Commentary on the *Paṇītatarasutta*, etc.

343–391. *Vissaṭṭhakāyā* means those who have relinquished their bodies through the resolve of a virtuous nature (*adhiṭṭhitasīlatā*) and a mind free from expectation, thinking: "Let whoever needs skin, blood, or bone take it all.

*Duvidhakārino* means those who perform both kinds [of actions], namely, doing what is wholesome at one time and what is unwholesome at another. *Saha byayati pavattati* means it proceeds and functions together.

A companion (*sahāya*), one who moves together; the state of that is companionship (*sahabyatā*), which is "companionship. That which is to be eaten is food (*anna*); that which is to be chewed is solid food (*khajja*);

that which is to be drunk is a beverage (*pāna*); that which is to be worn is clothing (*vattha*); that which is to be put on is an undergarment (*nivāsana*); that which is to be wrapped around is an upper garment (*pāvuraṇa*).

It is called a vehicle (*yāna*) because one goes by means of it, such as vehicles like sandals and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of bullock-carts, palanquins, and the like.
Having established that the parasol is a means for traveling on the path by way of protection from the suffering of heat and dangers, it is said, "the parasol and sandals," and so forth.
Therefore it is stated, "whatever is a requisite for travel. Having made a resolution...
[and so on] ...it should be understood that they are reborn there, like the Nāga king Campeyya.
The commentary on the Paṇītatarasutta and others is finished.
The commentary on the Nāgasaṃyutta is finished.
9. The commentary on the Supaṇṇasaṃyutta.
392–437. “*Pattānan*” means of those who have reached both sides. “*Vaṇṇavantatāyā*” means by way of possessing an exceedingly variegated color;
for this word *vanta* has the sense of “exceedingly. “*By the method previously stated*” means by the method described in the first sutta of the *Nāgasaṃyutta*.
“*They lift up*” means they lift them from the ocean; however, their lifting from within the earth or from between mountains is [also implied].
"It is indeed difficult. "More excellent" means more excellent by way of strength; that is, they are powerful.
"Elephants that cannot be lifted up" refers to elephants that are impossible to lift because of their great majesty and because their dwelling places are inaccessible.
Having stated that there are "seven kinds," he says "Kambalassataras," etc., showing them both by their specific names and by their dwelling places.
In this context, "the Kambalas, Assataras, and Dhataratthas" are mentioned by way of their birth.

"The dwellers in the seven seas of Sīdanta" means those who live in the seven kinds of Sīda oceans. "The earth-dwellers" (pathaviṭṭhakā) are those who live within the earth; likewise for the "mountain-dwellers.
And these are the inhabitants of celestial mansions (vimāna). The connection is that no supaṇṇa is able to lift up those nāgas. "The rest" refers to...
Regarding the passage beginning with “those who act dually with the body,” everything that needs to be said follows the same method as that explained in the *Nāga-saṃyutta*;
and it is the intention [of the commentator] that the meaning should be understood according to the method stated therein.
The commentary on the *Supaṇṇa-saṃyutta* is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Gandhabbakāyasaṃyutta* (438–549).
They protect and employ scents distinguished as root-scent and so forth; thus they are *gandhabbas*. Their body, or their multitude, is the *gandhabbakāya*, meaning the class of *gandhabba* deities.
They are to be seen as a specific group among the Cātumahārājika devas, because they are included therein.
Those who are attached to that [place] are the *gandhabba*-class beings.

The scent that arises depending on the roots of various trees, shrubs, and creepers is "root-scent" (*mūlagandha*); [they dwell] in that root-scent. "Dwelling there" (*adhivatthā*) means dwelling having established themselves upon or having overcome that root-scent.
This same method applies to the others as well. "Depending on that" means depending on that tree, which is the root-scent, as a condition.
[They] were produced having been made [so]. Showing that it is not only the scent there, nor even just the root, that is their requisite condition, he said "So hi" and so forth.
"It serves" (upakappati) means it is employed as a place of residence. "In the collection of scents" (gandhagandhe) means in the mass of scents. "In the scent of the scents of roots, etc.
(mūlādigandhānaṃ gandhe) means in the scent of the constituent parts contained within the roots, etc.; [it refers to] that which has become a collection consisting of the roots, etc.
The meaning is as follows. Previously, by the phrase "the scent of the root" (*mūlagandha*) and so forth, the scent of the individual parts of trees was taken;
however, here, because it is taken in its entirety, it should be understood as the scent of the whole (*samudāyagandha*). Therefore he said, "Of whichever tree... and so forth.

"That" (*so*) refers to that entire collection of scents residing in the roots and other parts; this is what is called "scent-of-scent" (*gandhagandha*) here. Of that scent, [the term] "scent" (*gandha*)...

Regarding that collective fragrance (*samudāyagandha*) and such a fragrance: "sarikkhadāna" means a gift that has a counterpart (*sarikkha*), that is, something similar (*sadisa*) or an equivalent offering (*paṭidāna*);
it refers to a wish. [The question is: "How can there be an 'asimilar gift' (*asarikkhadāna*) when the intended fruits should give their intended fruit precisely because they are similar gifts?
To this he says, "Even an asimilar gift," and so forth, meaning that even such a gift gives all desired things because merit (*puñña*) grants everything one wishes for.
The commentary on the *Gandhabbakāya-saṃyutta* is finished.
11. Commentary on the *Valāhaka-saṃyutta* (550–606).
They are called *valāha* because they choose (*vāla*), restrain (*vara*), cover (*chāda*), and seek out food (*ahana*). They are sons of the gods.

The collection of these is called the "host of cloud-deities" (*valāhakadevakāya*); thus he says, "those belonging to the cloud-host" (*valāhakakāyikā*), and so forth. "Clouds that produce cold" means clouds that remove cold.

"In the remaining phrases" refers to the phrases beginning with "clouds that produce heat" (*uṇhavalāhakā*). "The same method applies" means the meaning should be understood through such expressions as "clouds that produce heat.
"Fixing the mind" (*cittaṭṭhapana*) means the generation of a thought such as, "Let it be cold. "During the rains" (*vassāne*) means during the rainy season.
"Utusamuṭṭhānameva" means simply the natural cold. "Uṇhepi" means even during the hot season. "Abbhamaṇḍapo" refers to a canopy made of layers of clouds resembling a pavilion.
"Abbhaṃ uppajjati" means that the layers arise here and there. "Abbheyyeva" means precisely during the time of clouds; that is, in the rainy season.
"Atiabbhaṃ" refers to the rising of clouds consisting of hundreds or thousands of layers. "Cittavesākhamāsesu" [means] in the months of Citta and Vesākha.
He speaks with reference to the spring season (*vasantakāla*). For at that time, it is appropriate for the cloudless sky to be pierced [by the wind].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "northern, southern, etc.," he includes the western wind and so forth. "Natural wind" (*pakativāta*) means the wind that blows by its own nature or inherent character.

He states that this is produced solely by the season (*utusamuṭṭhāna*); that is, it is produced by the season which is the common kamma-proximate cause (*sādhāraṇakammūpanissaya*) for beings who subsist on nutriment.

This same principle applies to cold, heat, and wind produced by the seasons (*utu-samuṭṭhāna*). For that too is solely due to the common kamma-support (*sādhāraṇa-kamma-upanissaya*) of beings who subsist on nutriment.
"Song" refers to the song of the clouds. "By an act of truth" means through the resolve upon truth (*sacca-adhiṭṭhāna*) of such distinguished persons.

"By the power of psychic potency" means by the majestic influence of the psychic powers (*iddhi-ānubhāva*) of those possessing such powers. "By a world-destroying cloud" means by a cloud that destroys the eon (*kappa-vināsaka-megha*). [The same applies] to others as well, for beings of dark and evil nature...
Due to the condition of evil karma, each respective region is destroyed when rained upon by the cloud that has arisen for destruction.
The commentary on the *Valāhakasaṃyutta* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *Vacchagottasaṃyutta*.
607–661. *Aññāṇā* means "due to ignorance"; the meaning is "due to the delusion that conceals the Truths.
However, in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), in order to show this very same meaning by using the instrumental case in the sense of a cause, it says "*aññāṇena*.
Regarding the phrase "all [these]": the terms "*aññāṇā*, *adassanā*, *anabhisamayā*" and so forth appear in eleven suttas; there are fifty-five [instances].
The *Veyyākaraṇas* have been explained, because the exposition (*veyyākaraṇa*) is found in the Suttas by way of the five aggregates (*pañca-khandha*).
The commentary on the *Vacchagotta-saṃyutta* is finished.
13. The *Jhāna-saṃyutta*.

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Attainment Rooted in Concentration (Samādhimūlakasamāpattisutta-vaṇṇanā) 662. "Skilled in concentration" means skilled regarding concentration. This skill in concentration, together with the application of the jhāna factors, is fourfold as jhāna-concentration;
therefore, it is established for one who knows its various divisions. Thus he says: "First..."
“Jhāna,” and so forth. Therein, the first [jhāna] has five factors by way of applied thought (vitakka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā);
the second has three factors by way of rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness; the third has two factors by way of bliss and one-pointedness;

and the fourth has exactly two factors by way of equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness. Thus, one is skilled in the determination of the respective factors in each respective jhāna. “Skilled in attainment” means:
"Skilled in attaining" means being proficient in entering [meditative absorption]. "Having gladdened" means having satisfied.
"Having made fit" means having made the mind capable of attaining absorption by removing the factors opposed to concentration and by providing the auxiliary causes for concentration.
"The remaining phrases" refers to the other three sections. In the third and subsequent methods, even one who is unskilled is called "a meditator" because they have set out for the sake of jhāna.
The commentary on the *Samādhimūlakasamāpatti-sutta* is finished.
2–55. Commentary on the *Samādhimūlaṭṭhiti-sutta* and others, 663–716.
Regarding the phrase "skilled in stability" (*ṭhitikusalo*) in the second and subsequent suttas: here, the word "stability" (*ṭhiti*) has the sense of a cause included within it; and in that regard—
But because it means "unskilled," he said, "unskilled in maintaining jhāna.

"For only seven or eight finger-snap moments" means that he is unable to maintain the jhāna for a duration of seven or eight finger-snap moments because he has not yet accomplished mastery over maintenance (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasī*).
He is unable to emerge at the predetermined time because he has not yet accomplished mastery over emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*).

"Fit to be born" means it is *kallita*; in that state of being fit (*kallita*), one who is unable to attain [jhāna] upon the kasiṇa objects by way of the object—thinking "this is for such-and-such a person"—is not skilled in the object regarding concentration.
"Not skilled in the resort regarding concentration" means [not skilled] in that resort known as the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) which is to be accomplished within concentration.
One who is devoid of mindfulness and clear comprehension in the place of activity and in the range of the alms-round is unskilled.

Some, however, say that one is called "unskilled" in regard to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) when they do not know how the first jhāna and so forth should be entered and how they should be cultivated—that is, the range of the meditation subject. To "lead out the meditation subject" means [to lead it] toward the state of partaking in distinction.
Unskilled in bringing forth [the attainment]. "One who acts with care" means one who treats it with respect. "One who acts with persistence" means one who acts with constancy.
"States that assist concentration" refers to skill in absorption (*appanā*). Regarding the phrase "by means of attainments, etc.," the word "etc.

should be understood as including the terms "one who acts with care" and so forth, because these are stated in sets of four. Therefore he said: "Having joined them, they are stated in sets of four. This is by way of mundane jhāna alone.
It has been stated [that he is] "skilled in concentration" and so forth, because the teaching proceeds in such a manner.

For indeed, no lack of skill (akosalla) can be found regarding supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). If there were a lack of skill, they would not need to be distinguished by the word "skillful" (kusala).
The commentary on the *Samādhimūlakaṭhitisutta* and others is concluded.
The commentary on the Jhāna Saṃyutta is finished.
And thus ends the commentary on the Khandha Vagga within the Sāratthappakāsinī, the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
